paragraphs.context: The map is not the land, my father often said
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jon explains to Stannis that the empty mountains on his map are in fact full of mountain clansmen, and describes their way of life.
paragraphs.simple: Jon tells Stannis that the map is not the land. Men have lived in the high valleys and mountain meadows for thousands of years, ruled by their clan chiefs. They are petty lords, Jon says, though they do not use such titles themselves. Their champions fight with huge two-handed greatswords, while common men sling stones and batter one another with staffs of mountain ash. A quarrelsome folk, it must be said. When they are not fighting one another, they tend their herds, fish the Bay of Ice, and breed the hardiest mounts you will ever ride.

paragraphs.context: It is no good sending messages. Your Grace will need
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jon advises Stannis to visit the mountain clans in person and win them with honor and hospitality, not with commands.
paragraphs.simple: Jon tells the king: ask, I said, not beg. It is no good sending messages. Your Grace will need to go to them yourself. Eat their bread and salt, drink their ale, listen to their pipers, praise the beauty of their daughters and the courage of their sons, and you will have their swords. The clans have not seen a king since Torrhen Stark bent his knee. Your coming does them honor. Command them to fight for you, and they will look at one another and say, “Who is this man? He is no king of mine.”

paragraphs.context: Hatred does not stir the stone men half so much
paragraphs.mainIdea: Haldon explains that the stone men attack out of hunger, not hatred: nothing to eat grows in the fog, and the food ships are often late.
paragraphs.simple: Haldon the Halfmaester explains: hatred does not stir the stone men half so much as hunger. Nothing any sane man would want to eat grows in these fogs. Thrice each year the triarchs of Volantis send a galley upriver with provisions, but the mercy ships are often late, and sometimes bring more mouths than food.

paragraphs.context: There are worse ways to die than drowning
paragraphs.mainIdea: Sinking into the river, Tyrion feels he already died in King’s Landing; only his vengeful ghost remains.
paragraphs.simple: As he sinks, Tyrion thinks there are worse ways to die than drowning. And if truth be told, he perished long ago, back in King’s Landing. It is only his revenant who remains: the small vengeful ghost who throttled Shae and put a crossbow bolt through the great Lord Tywin’s bowels. No man would mourn the thing that he has become. He will haunt the Seven Kingdoms, he thinks, sinking deeper. They would not love him living, so let them dread him dead.

paragraphs.context: A thousand years before the Conquest, a promise was made, and oaths
paragraphs.mainIdea: Little Wylla reminds the court of the ancient oath: the Manderlys swore to serve the Starks forever.
paragraphs.simple: The girl Wylla insists she knows about the promise. A thousand years before the Conquest, a promise was made, and oaths were sworn in the Wolf’s Den before the old gods and the new. When the Manderlys were sore beset and friendless, hounded from their homes and in peril of their lives, the wolves took them in and nourished them and protected them against their enemies. The city is built upon the land they gave them. In return the Manderlys swore that they should always be their men. Stark men!

paragraphs.context: He made Lady Hornwood marry him, then shut her
paragraphs.mainIdea: Wylla tells the court of Ramsay’s cruelty to Lady Hornwood: forced marriage, a dungeon, and starvation.
paragraphs.simple: Wylla cries out that Ramsay will never be her lord. He made Lady Hornwood marry him, then shut her in a dungeon and made her eat her fingers.

paragraphs.context: Seven, he thought, seven fingers. A man can make
paragraphs.mainIdea: Reek thinks about the price Ramsay made him pay: his fingers, cut off one by one.
paragraphs.simple: Reek knew the cost. Seven, he thought, seven fingers. A man can make do with seven fingers. Seven is a sacred number. He remembered how much it had hurt when Lord Ramsay had commanded Skinner to lay his ring finger bare.

paragraphs.context: Ralf Kenning lay shivering beneath a mountain of furs
paragraphs.mainIdea: The ironborn commander is dying: wounded, feverish, rotting under furs, with his weapons stacked beside him.
paragraphs.simple: Ralf Kenning lay shivering beneath a mountain of furs. His arms were stacked beside him — sword and axe, mail hauberk, iron warhelm. His shield bore the storm god’s cloudy hand, lightning crackling from his fingers down to a raging sea, but the paint was discolored and peeling, the wood beneath starting to rot.

paragraphs.context: The dam broke then. Halleck was a man of
paragraphs.mainIdea: Once the respected Halleck joins Jon, the others follow: the wildlings follow strength, not names or titles.
paragraphs.simple: The dam broke then. Halleck was a man of note. Mance was not wrong. “Free folk don’t follow names, or little cloth animals sewn on a tunic,” the King-Beyond-the-Wall had told Jon. “They won’t dance for coins, they don’t care how you style yourself or what that chain of office means or who your grandsire was. They follow strength. They follow the man.”

paragraphs.context: You’ve added sixty-three more mouths, my lord … but
paragraphs.mainIdea: Marsh warns Jon that the new recruits are sixty-three more mouths to feed — and no one knows whose side they would fight on.
paragraphs.simple: Marsh was unconvinced. “You’ve added sixty-three more mouths, my lord … but how many are fighters, and whose side will they fight on? If it’s the Others at the gates, most like they’ll stand with us, I grant you … but if it’s Tormund Giantsbane or the Weeping Man come calling with ten thousand howling killers, what then?”

paragraphs.context: Westeros is torn and bleeding, and I do
paragraphs.mainIdea: Tyrion urges Aegon to sail west at once: Cersei is destroying her own alliances, and men will flock to a new Targaryen — but the moment will not last.
paragraphs.simple: Tyrion tells the prince that Westeros is torn and bleeding, and he does not doubt that even now his sweet sister is binding up the wounds … with salt. Cersei is as gentle as King Maegor, as selfless as Aegon the Unworthy, as wise as Mad Aerys. She never forgets a slight, real or imagined. She takes caution for cowardice and dissent for defiance. And she is greedy: greedy for power, for honor, for love. Tommen’s rule is bolstered by all of the alliances that Tyrion’s lord father built so carefully, but soon enough she will destroy them, every one. Land and raise your banners, and men will flock to your cause — lords great and small, and smallfolk too. But do not wait too long, my prince. The moment will not last. The tide that lifts you now will soon recede. Be certain you reach Westeros before his sister falls and someone more competent takes her place.

paragraphs.context: Benerro has sent forth the word from Volantis
paragraphs.mainIdea: The red priest Benerro preaches that Daenerys fulfills an ancient prophecy: Azor Ahai returned, bringing a summer that will never end.
paragraphs.simple: Haldon nods. Benerro has sent forth the word from Volantis. Her coming is the fulfillment of an ancient prophecy. From smoke and salt was she born to make the world anew. She is Azor Ahai returned … and her triumph over darkness will bring a summer that will never end … death itself will bend its knee, and all those who die fighting in her cause shall be reborn.

paragraphs.context: You need a king beside you to help
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Green Grace tells Dany she seems too young and frail to rule alone — she needs a king to share her burdens.
paragraphs.simple: The priestess says she has often heard Dany call herself only a young girl. To look at her, she still seems half a child, too young and frail to face such trials by herself. You need a king beside you to help you bear these burdens.

paragraphs.context: He shall be the stallion that mounts the world
paragraphs.mainIdea: Dany recalls the prophecy about her unborn son — and Mirri Maz Duur’s curse, which means she will never bear a living child.
paragraphs.simple: He shall be the stallion that mounts the world. Dany knew how it went with prophecies. They were made of words, and words were wind. There would be no son for Loraq, no heir to unite dragon and harpy. When the sun rises in the west and sets in the east, when the seas go dry and mountains blow in the wind like leaves — only then would her womb quicken once again.

paragraphs.context: Then winkle them out of their pyramids on some
paragraphs.mainIdea: Daario proposes a massacre: use a wedding as a pretext to gather the Great Masters, then set his men loose on them.
paragraphs.simple: Daario tells Dany to winkle the Great Masters out of their pyramids on some pretext. A wedding might serve. Why not? Promise her hand to Hizdahr and all the Great Masters will come to see her married. When they gather in the Temple of the Graces, turn his men loose upon them.

paragraphs.context: We will not be alone. Dorne will join
paragraphs.mainIdea: Griff argues that Dorne must join Aegon’s cause — because Aegon is Elia’s son as well as Rhaegar’s.
paragraphs.simple: Griff had heard enough of the captain-general’s cowardice. “We will not be alone. Dorne will join us, must join us. Prince Aegon is Elia’s son as well as Rhaegar’s.”

paragraphs.context: Death, he knew, but slow. I still have
paragraphs.mainIdea: Griff accepts he is dying of greyscale — slowly — but hopes he has one to five years left to finish his mission.
paragraphs.simple: Death, he knew, but slow. I still have time. A year. Two years. Five. Some stone men live for ten. Time enough to cross the sea, to see Griffin’s Roost again. To end the Usurper’s line for good and all, and put Rhaegar’s son upon the Iron Throne.

paragraphs.context: Even the commander of the Windblown kept his true
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Tattered Prince’s history: chosen to be prince of Pentos, he fled instead and became a sellsword, founding the Windblown.
paragraphs.simple: Even the commander of the Windblown kept his true name to himself. The Windblown went back thirty years, and had known but one commander: the soft-spoken, sad-eyed Pentoshi nobleman called the Tattered Prince. His hair and mail were silver-grey, but his ragged cloak was made of twists of cloth of many colors, all faded by the sun. When the Tattered Prince was three-and-twenty, the magisters of Pentos had chosen him to be their new prince, hours after beheading their old prince. Instead he’d buckled on a sword, mounted his favorite horse, and fled to the Disputed Lands, never to return. He had ridden with the Second Sons, the Iron Shields, and the Maiden’s Men, then joined with five brothers-in-arms to form the Windblown. Of those six founders, only he survived.

paragraphs.context: We’re all Seven Kingdoms born here. M’lord never broke up the
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Westerosi sellswords grow suspicious: why send all the Westeros-born men together on this mission?
paragraphs.simple: Dick Straw cleared his throat. “Begging your pardon, but we’re all Seven Kingdoms born here. M’lord never broke up the company by blood or tongue before. Why send us lot together?”

paragraphs.context: This is poison that I hold, she thought
paragraphs.mainIdea: Asha receives a raven letter with bad news: the northmen have taken Moat Cailin.
paragraphs.simple: This is poison that I hold, Asha thought. I ought to burn it. Instead she cracked the seal. A scrap of leather fluttered down into her lap. When she read the dry brown words, her black mood grew blacker still. Dark wings, dark words. The ravens never brought glad tidings. The last message sent to Deepwood had been from Stannis Baratheon, demanding homage. This was worse. “The northmen have taken Moat Cailin.”

paragraphs.context: Torgon Greyiron was the king’s eldest son. But the
paragraphs.mainIdea: Tris tells the old story of Torgon the Latecomer: a kingsmoot held in his absence chose another king, who then killed the old king’s sons.
paragraphs.simple: Tris tells the tale. Torgon Greyiron was the king’s eldest son. But the king was old and Torgon restless, so it happened that when his father died he was raiding along the Mander from his stronghold on Greyshield. His brothers sent no word to him but instead quickly called a kingsmoot, thinking that one of them would be chosen to wear the driftwood crown. But the captains and the kings chose Urragon Goodbrother to rule instead. The first thing the new king did was command that all the sons of the old king be put to death, and so they were. After that men called him Badbrother, though in truth they’d been no kin of his. He ruled for almost two years.

paragraphs.context: That Daenerys stands in peril. The dark eye has
paragraphs.mainIdea: Benerro preaches that Daenerys is in danger: the dark eye watches her, and the servants of night plot her destruction.
paragraphs.simple: The priest cries out that Daenerys stands in peril. The dark eye has fallen upon her, and the minions of night are plotting her destruction, praying to their false gods in temples of deceit … conspiring at betrayal with godless outlanders.

paragraphs.context: At the bridge’s center span, the severed hands of
paragraphs.mainIdea: On the Long Bridge, the severed hands and heads of criminals are displayed as a warning, with guards waving birds away.
paragraphs.simple: At the bridge’s center span, the severed hands of thieves and cutpurses hung like strings of onions from iron stanchions along the roadway. Three heads were on display as well — two men and a woman, their crimes scrawled on tablets underneath them. A pair of spearmen attended them, clad in polished helms and shirts of silver mail. Across their cheeks were tiger stripes as green as jade. From time to time the guards waved their spears to chase away the kestrels, gulls, and carrion crows paying court to the deceased. The birds returned to the heads within moments.

paragraphs.context: I have no sister. Only brothers. Only you
paragraphs.mainIdea: Reading that Ramsay will marry “Arya Stark,” Jon forces himself to say he has no sister — though the words hurt him.
paragraphs.simple: By now she’d be eleven, Jon thought. Still a child. “I have no sister. Only brothers. Only you.” He says this to Mormont’s raven, but Lady Catelyn would have rejoiced to hear those words, he knew. That did not make them easier to say. His fingers closed around the parchment. Would that they could crush Ramsay Bolton’s throat as easily.

paragraphs.context: Nine crows flew into the white wood to find
paragraphs.mainIdea: Melisandre warns Jon that of the nine rangers he sent out, three are already dead — and offers to save his “sister” if he takes her hand.
paragraphs.simple: Melisandre rises, her red robes stirring in the wind. “Hear me now, Jon Snow. Nine crows flew into the white wood to find your foes for you. Three of them are dead. They have not died yet, but their death is out there waiting for them, and they ride to meet it. You sent them forth to be your eyes in the darkness, but they will be eyeless when they return to you. I have seen their pale dead faces in my flames. Empty sockets, weeping blood.” Jon does not believe her. “You will,” she says. “The cost of that belief will be three lives.” And when that day comes, he should take her hand — and let her save his sister.

paragraphs.context: I have treated you most shamefully, I know. I
paragraphs.mainIdea: Freed from his cell, Davos learns Manderly’s cruelty was an act: his son Wylis is home, and the feast celebrates his return.
paragraphs.simple: Lord Wyman sighed. “I have treated you most shamefully, I know. I had my reasons, but … please, sit and drink, I beg you. Drink to my boy’s safe return. Wylis, my eldest son and heir. He is home. That is the welcoming feast you hear. In the Merman’s Court they are eating lamprey pie and venison with roasted chestnuts. Wynafryd is dancing with the Frey she is to marry. The other Freys are raising cups of wine to toast our friendship.”

paragraphs.context: Was ever snow so black? asked Lord Wyman
paragraphs.mainIdea: Manderly describes Ramsay’s evil: he seized the Hornwood lands by forced marriage, then let his wife starve until she ate her own fingers — and King’s Landing rewards him with a Stark bride.
paragraphs.simple: “Was ever snow so black?” asked Lord Wyman. “Ramsay took Lord Hornwood’s lands by forcibly wedding his widow, then locked her in a tower and forgot her. It is said she ate her own fingers in her extremity … and the Lannister notion of king’s justice is to reward her killer with Ned Stark’s little girl.”

paragraphs.context: His horse was bleeding, Grey Worm said
paragraphs.mainIdea: The rider’s horse was bleeding from the bowels — a sign of the pale mare, the bloody flux.
paragraphs.simple: “His horse was bleeding, Grey Worm said.” “This thing is true, Your Grace,” the eunuch confirmed. “The pale mare was bloody between the legs.” “That may be so, Your Radiance,” said Ezzara, “but this blood was mingled with loose stool.” “He was bleeding from the bowels,” said Galazza Galare.

paragraphs.context: Outside our walls, the Yunkai’i devoured our crops and
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Astapori refugees tell of starvation: they ate cats, rats, leather, and finally drew lots to eat one another.
paragraphs.simple: The cobbler went on. “Outside our walls, the Yunkai’i devoured our crops and slaughtered our herds. Inside we starved. We ate cats and rats and leather. A horsehide was a feast. King Cutthroat and Queen Whore accused each other of feasting on the flesh of the slain. Men and women gathered in secret to draw lots and gorge upon the flesh of him who drew the black stone.”

paragraphs.context: Must I wear the bloody bones as well?
paragraphs.mainIdea: The wildling describes how the ruby glamor feels: warm like a kiss in sleep, but burning in dreams.
paragraphs.simple: “The glamor, aye.” In the black iron fetter about his wrist, the ruby seemed to pulse. He tapped it with the edge of his blade. “I feel it when I sleep. Warm against my skin, even through the iron. Soft as a woman’s kiss. Your kiss. But sometimes in my dreams it starts to burn, and your lips turn into teeth. Every day I think how easy it would be to pry it out, and every day I don’t. Must I wear the bloody bones as well?”

paragraphs.context: But the widow’s peak dissolved. The brown mustache, the
paragraphs.mainIdea: Melisandre speaks a word and the glamor falls away: the Lord of Bones’ face melts into Mance Rayder’s.
paragraphs.simple: But the widow’s peak dissolved. The brown mustache, the knobby chin, the sallow yellowed flesh and small dark eyes, all melted. Grey fingers crept through long brown hair. Laugh lines appeared at the corners of his mouth. All at once he was bigger than before, broader in the chest and shoulders, long-legged and lean, his face clean-shaved and windburnt.

paragraphs.context: You did not find our missing Freys
paragraphs.mainIdea: Roose notes, with quiet menace, that Ramsay’s hunt never found the three vanished Freys.
paragraphs.simple: “You did not find our missing Freys.” The way Roose Bolton said it, it was more a statement than a question.

paragraphs.context: Ramsay killed him. A sickness of the bowels, Maester
paragraphs.mainIdea: Roose believes Ramsay poisoned his trueborn son Domeric, who only wanted a brother by his side.
paragraphs.simple: “Ramsay killed him. A sickness of the bowels, Maester Uthor says, but I say poison. In the Vale, Domeric had enjoyed the company of Redfort’s sons. He wanted a brother by his side, so he rode up the Weeping Water to seek my bastard out. I forbade it, but Domeric was a man grown and thought that he knew better than his father. Now his bones lie beneath the Dreadfort with the bones of his brothers, who died still in the cradle, and I am left with Ramsay.”

paragraphs.context: His blood is on my sister’s hands, and
paragraphs.mainIdea: Tyrion answers Penny’s accusation: he has killed many, but never a juggler or a dwarf — her brother’s death is not his fault.
paragraphs.simple: The accusation stung, coming so hard on the heels of Jorah Mormont’s words. “His blood is on my sister’s hands, and the hands of the brutes who killed him. My hands …” Tyrion turned them over, inspected them, coiled them into fists. “… my hands are crusted with old blood, aye. Call me kinslayer, and you won’t be wrong. Kingslayer, I’ll answer to that one as well. I have killed mothers, fathers, nephews, lovers, men and women, kings and whores. A singer once annoyed me, so I had the bastard stewed. But I have never killed a juggler, nor a dwarf, and I am not to blame for what happened to your bloody brother.”

paragraphs.context: His own father sold him to a slaver when
paragraphs.mainIdea: Penny tells of her grandfather: sold to a slaver at three, he became a famous mummer and bought his own freedom.
paragraphs.simple: Penny tells the story. Their father was a little person, but their mother was not. Their father’s own father sold him to a slaver when he was three. But he grew up to be such a famous mummer that he bought his freedom. He traveled to all the Free Cities, and Westeros as well. In Oldtown they used to call him Hop-Bean.

paragraphs.context: Abomination. That had always been Haggon’s favorite word. Abomination, abomination,
paragraphs.mainIdea: Haggon taught Varamyr the three great taboos of skinchanging: eating human flesh, mating as a wolf with wolves, and stealing another man's body — the last being the worst of all.
paragraphs.simple: Varamyr's teacher Haggon said a skinchanger must never eat people, live as a wolf's mate, or take over another person's body.

paragraphs.context: Varamyr might have been amongst them if only he’d been
paragraphs.mainIdea: Varamyr is dying his true death — he has already 'died' nine times inside his beasts. The squirrel-skin cloak line recalls the petty theft that got him stabbed.
paragraphs.simple: Varamyr knows he will die for good this time. He has died nine times before when his animals died. He was stabbed while stealing a cheap fur cloak from a dead woman.

paragraphs.context: Haggon’s rough voice echoed in his head. “You will die
paragraphs.mainIdea: Haggon promised that a skinchanger's true death is not the end: his spirit lives on inside a beast, a simpler and sweeter 'second life.'
paragraphs.simple: Haggon said you can die many times, but when your true death comes, you live again inside an animal.

paragraphs.context: Dogs were the easiest beasts to bond with; they lived
paragraphs.mainIdea: Skinchanging lore: dogs accept a human spirit easily, like an old boot accepts a foot; wolves are harder — bonding with a wolf is like a marriage that changes both forever.
paragraphs.simple: Dogs are easy to enter because they live close to people. Wolves are hard: once you bond with a wolf, you become part of each other.

paragraphs.context: He summoned all the strength still in him, leapt out
paragraphs.mainIdea: Dying, Varamyr breaks Haggon's greatest taboo: he forces his spirit out of his own body and into Thistle's living flesh to escape death.
paragraphs.simple: Varamyr does the worst forbidden thing: he jumps out of his dying body and into Thistle's body.

paragraphs.context: The white world turned and fell away. For a moment
paragraphs.mainIdea: As his body dies, Varamyr's spirit floods through the whole forest — owl, hare, trees, worms — exulting 'I am the wood, and everything that's in it,' before seeking his wolves for his second life.
paragraphs.simple: As Varamyr dies, his spirit spreads into everything in the forest. He is joyful: 'I am the wood.' Then he looks for his wolves.

paragraphs.context: The wine has blurred my wits. He had learned to
paragraphs.mainIdea: Tyrion notes the Free Cities don't really share one 'Valyrian' — they speak nine diverging dialects, and he only knows scraps of some of them.
paragraphs.simple: The nine Free Cities each speak a different kind of Valyrian. Tyrion knows a little of some, but not enough.

paragraphs.context: “Wherever whores go,” his father had said. His last words,
paragraphs.mainIdea: 'Wherever whores go' — Tywin's last words — haunts Tyrion; he keeps reliving the murder and his father's contempt, even in death.
paragraphs.simple: Tyrion cannot stop thinking about his father's last words and killing him. Even dead, his father seems to despise him.

paragraphs.context: “This is so,” Illyrio agreed, “but the world is one
paragraphs.mainIdea: Illyrio's web metaphor: the world is so connected that touching one strand shakes all the others — news from distant Slaver's Bay matters in Pentos.
paragraphs.simple: Illyrio says the world is like a spider web: everything is connected, so far-away events shake everything.

paragraphs.context: The cheesemonger spooned up cherries. “In Volantis they use a
paragraphs.mainIdea: Illyrio's coin metaphor: a coin has a crown on one face and a death's-head on the other — making Myrcella queen is the same act as killing her.
paragraphs.simple: Illyrio says crowning Myrcella and killing her are two sides of the same coin — you cannot do one without the other.

paragraphs.context: “What one king does, another may undo. In Pentos we
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Prince of Pentos lives in luxury — but if a harvest fails or a war is lost, the city cuts his throat as a sacrifice to the gods and picks a new prince.
paragraphs.simple: Pentos has a prince who lives like a king, but if things go badly the people kill him and choose a new one.

paragraphs.context: Dothraki were wise where horses were concerned, but could be
paragraphs.mainIdea: Dany reflects on her Dothraki handmaids — girls her own age, given to her at her wedding — and the lion pelt Drogo gave her, which she wears to feel close to him.
paragraphs.simple: Dany's servants are girls her age, a wedding gift from Drogo. She wears the lion skin he gave her to feel near him.

paragraphs.context: Dany had wanted to ban the tokar when she took
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Green Grace warns Dany: to rule Meereen she must wear the Meereenese tokar — otherwise she will always be seen as a hated foreign conqueror.
paragraphs.simple: Dany's advisor says she must dress like the Meereenese, or the people will always hate her as a stranger.

paragraphs.context: “You have no lack of enemies, Your Grace. You can
paragraphs.mainIdea: Skahaz names Dany's real enemies: the old slaving families, above all House Pahl — 'a house of women now. Bitter old women with a taste for blood. Women do not forget. Women do not forgive.'
paragraphs.simple: Skahaz lists the great families fighting Dany. The Pahl family is now run by bitter old women who will never forgive her.

paragraphs.context: Reznak would have summoned another tokar next, but Dany insisted
paragraphs.mainIdea: As queen, Dany spends her days hearing grievances: masters and freedmen both demand redress for the violence of the sack of Meereen.
paragraphs.simple: Every day Dany listens to people complaining about wrongs from the war. Both masters and freed slaves want justice.

paragraphs.context: “Snow,” the moon called down again, cackling. The white wolf
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jon's wolf dream: as the white wolf he remembers his lost litter-mates — once six pups, now four remain, and one he can no longer sense.
paragraphs.simple: In his dream Jon is a white wolf. He remembers there were six wolf pups once, but now one is gone.

paragraphs.context: Burning dead children had ceased to trouble Jon Snow; live
paragraphs.mainIdea: Melisandre wants 'king's blood' for her magic — burning Mance's infant son — and even Aemon warns Jon that Stannis might allow it.
paragraphs.simple: Melisandre may burn a baby for magic because it has 'king's blood.' Even the wise old maester fears Stannis would let her.

paragraphs.context: Stannis read from the letter. “Bear Island knows no king
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ten-year-old Lyanna Mormont's defiant letter: Bear Island knows no king but a Stark — she scolds King Stannis to his face.
paragraphs.simple: A ten-year-old girl writes to King Stannis: we only follow the Starks. She dares to scold a king.

paragraphs.context: “Do not be so certain.” The ruby at Melisandre’s throat
paragraphs.mainIdea: Melisandre's warning and prophecy: Jon's true enemies are not the ones who curse him openly but smiling traitors — 'Ice, I see, and daggers in the dark.'
paragraphs.simple: Melisandre warns Jon: fear the people who smile at you and hide knives. She sees ice and daggers in her fire.

paragraphs.context: Other times, when he was tired of being a wolf,
paragraphs.mainIdea: Bran sometimes slips his mind into Hodor's body — the gentle giant whimpers and thrashes in fear, and Bran can taste Hodor's terror — a dark echo of the 'abomination' taboo.
paragraphs.simple: Sometimes Bran takes over Hodor's body. Hodor is frightened and shakes, but Bran does it anyway.

paragraphs.context: The ranger studied his hands as if he had never
paragraphs.mainIdea: Coldhands explains his black hands: when a man's heart stops, blood sinks and thickens in the hands and feet, turning them black as pudding.
paragraphs.simple: Coldhands says his hands are black because he is dead: when the heart stops, blood sinks down and turns black.

paragraphs.context: “He’s dead.” Bran could taste the bile in his throat.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Bran realizes Coldhands is a wight — a dead thing — and recalls Old Nan's rule: the dead cannot pass the Wall while the Night's Watch stays true.
paragraphs.simple: Bran understands Coldhands is dead. Old Nan said dead things cannot cross the Wall while the Watch is true.

paragraphs.context: “Viserys was Mad Aerys’s son, just so. Daenerys … Daenerys
paragraphs.mainIdea: Illyrio's verdict on Dany: the frightened child died on the Dothraki sea and was 'reborn in blood and fire' — she is a true Targaryen, nothing like her brother Viserys.
paragraphs.simple: Illyrio says Dany changed completely: the scared girl died, and a strong dragon queen was born. She is not like her mad brother.

paragraphs.context: The dwarf pondered that. The Golden Company was reputedly the
paragraphs.mainIdea: History of the Golden Company: founded by Bittersteel to keep exiled Blackfyre supporters together after their rebellion failed — exiles and sons of exiles, still dreaming of Westeros.
paragraphs.simple: The Golden Company was started by exiles who lost a war in Westeros. For a hundred years they have dreamed of going home.

paragraphs.context: Andalos. The Faith taught that the Seven themselves had once
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Faith's myth of Andalos: the Father plucked seven stars from the sky and set them on Hugor's brow as a glowing crown — the origin of the Seven's crown.
paragraphs.simple: The Faith teaches that the god took seven stars from the sky and made a shining crown for the first king.

paragraphs.context: Crawl back to Sunspear defeated, with my tail between my
paragraphs.mainIdea: Quentyn refuses to give up: he cannot crawl home defeated — his father's disappointment and the Sand Snakes' scorn would be unbearable; Doran entrusted Dorne's fate to him.
paragraphs.simple: Quentyn will not go home a failure. His father trusted him with Dorne's future, and he cannot bear to disappoint him.

paragraphs.context: “The triarchs are neither kings nor princes. Volantis is a
paragraphs.mainIdea: How Volantis is ruled: a freehold where all freeborn landowners share power — even women may vote — and three triarchs are elected from old Valyrian families for one-year terms.
paragraphs.simple: Volantis is ruled by landowners who all vote, even women. Three leaders are chosen each year from old families.

paragraphs.context: “Refuse, and the boy will burn. Not on the morrow,
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jon's terrible choice: Gilly must smuggle Mance's baby away, because once Mance is burned, Melisandre will claim the boy's 'king's blood' for her fires.
paragraphs.simple: Jon tells Gilly to take the baby far away. If she refuses, Melisandre will burn the child for magic.

paragraphs.context: “I found mention of dragonglass. The children of the forest
paragraphs.mainIdea: Sam's research on the Others: they come with the cold, wear armor no ordinary blade can pierce, shatter steel with icy swords — but fire dismays them and dragonglass kills them; the dead they slay rise again unless burned.
paragraphs.simple: Sam learned the Others wear armor swords cannot cut. Fire and dragonglass can kill them. Their victims become undead unless burned.

paragraphs.context: Kill the boy, Jon thought. The boy in you, and
paragraphs.mainIdea: 'Kill the boy' — Jon's hard farewell to Sam: to be men of the Night's Watch, both of them must kill the frightened boy inside.
paragraphs.simple: Jon sends Sam away with hard words: they must both kill the scared boy inside themselves and grow up.

paragraphs.context: Lord Tywin had put an end to that hope ten
paragraphs.mainIdea: Tywin's cruelty: he crushed boy Tyrion's wish to travel by sneering 'Neither ever wed a whore' — then punished him with charge of the castle's drains, and warned 'No man is free.'
paragraphs.simple: When young Tyrion wanted to travel, his father mocked him and gave him the sewers to clean as punishment.

paragraphs.context: Griff’s cloak was made from the hide and head of
paragraphs.mainIdea: Griff's description hides a clue: though his hair is dyed blue like his 'son's,' his roots and eyebrows are red — the dye is a disguise.
paragraphs.simple: Griff's blue hair is dyed: you can see red roots and red eyebrows. He is hiding who he really is.

paragraphs.context: “Storms.” Lord Godric said the word as fondly as another
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Sisters' old gods: the Lady of the Waves and the Lord of the Skies, who 'made storms every time they mated' — storms were sacred there before the Andals came.
paragraphs.simple: The old gods of the Sisters were the sea and the sky. People believed storms were made when the two gods mated.

paragraphs.context: Not as treacherous as men, thought Davos. Lord Godric’s forebears
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Sistermen's dark secret: their warning beacons are supposed to guide ships to safety, but on stormy nights some use false lights to lure ships onto the rocks and loot them.
paragraphs.simple: The people of the Sisters light false fires on the shore to trick ships into crashing, so they can steal from them.

paragraphs.context: He is stone and she is flame. The king’s eyes
paragraphs.mainIdea: 'He is stone and she is flame' — Stannis cold and hard beside Melisandre's fire; even Val in plain bronze looks more regal than the crowned king.
paragraphs.simple: Stannis is cold like stone, Melisandre is hot like flame. The wildling Val looks more like a queen than Stannis looks like a king.

paragraphs.context: One arrow took Mance Rayder in the chest, one in
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jon shows mercy by shooting the burning Mance with arrows — 'And now his Watch is done,' Jon murmurs, echoing the Night's Watch farewell for a fallen brother.
paragraphs.simple: Jon kills Mance quickly with arrows to end his pain. His words are the Watch's goodbye to a dead brother.

paragraphs.context: But most came on. Behind them was only cold and
paragraphs.mainIdea: The wildlings surrender to Stannis's god: 'the new god devoured the corpse of the old' as they feed their idols to the flames — cold and death behind them, hope ahead.
paragraphs.simple: The wildlings burn their old gods' wooden statues for the new fire god. Behind them is death; ahead is hope.

paragraphs.context: “Goghor speaks for us all.” The Spotted Cat wore a
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Spotted Cat's bitter irony: as a slave he slept on furs and ate meat; now free, he sleeps on straw and eats salt fish — freedom brought him poverty.
paragraphs.simple: A freed fighter says life was better as a slave: then he ate meat, now he eats fish and sleeps on straw.

paragraphs.context: Mother of dragons, Daenerys thought. Mother of monsters. What have
paragraphs.mainIdea: Dany's despair: 'Mother of dragons... Mother of monsters. What have I unleashed upon the world?' — her throne is built on burned bones and rests on quicksand.
paragraphs.simple: Dany fears her dragons are monsters and she is one too. Her power is built on death and may sink like sand.

paragraphs.context: Reek? Tears ran down his cheeks. “I remember. I do.”
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ramsay has broken Theon: he has forgotten his own name and must chant 'My name is Reek. It rhymes with leek' to remember the slave-name forced on him.
paragraphs.simple: Theon has forgotten who he is. He repeats his new slave name, Reek, to remember it.

paragraphs.context: “No. No, my lord, I swear.” Reek had tried to
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ramsay's torture: he never simply cuts — he flays skin and lets it fester until victims beg him to cut the limb off; Reek once tried to bite his own finger off to end the pain.
paragraphs.simple: Ramsay peels the skin off instead of cutting. The pain is so bad that Reek once tried to bite his own finger off.

paragraphs.context: “The First Men named us children,” the little woman said.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Leaf explains the children of the forest: not children or squirrels — their true name means 'those who sing the song of earth,' and they sang ten thousand years before men spoke.
paragraphs.simple: The little woman says her people are not children. Their real name means 'those who sing the song of earth.'

paragraphs.context: “A … crow?” The pale lord’s voice was dry. His
paragraphs.mainIdea: The three-eyed crow revealed: a former Night's Watch brother — 'Black of garb and black of blood' — who has watched Bran since birth with 'a thousand eyes and one.'
paragraphs.simple: The old man was once in the Night's Watch. He says he has watched Bran all his life, even when Bran fell.

paragraphs.context: All that ended abruptly the day his father returned from
paragraphs.mainIdea: Tywin's contempt for Tyrion: when boy Tyrion walked the feast table on his hands to make people laugh, Tywin sneered, 'You were born a lion, not a monkey.'
paragraphs.simple: Little Tyrion did tricks to make people laugh. His father said coldly: you are a lion, not a monkey.

paragraphs.context: “Volantis is the oldest of the Nine Free Cities, first
paragraphs.mainIdea: Young Griff's history lesson: Volantis, first daughter of Valyria, split into two factions after the Doom — the 'tigers' who wanted conquest by the sword, the 'elephants' who wanted wealth by trade.
paragraphs.simple: After Valyria fell, Volantis split into two groups: the tigers wanted war, the elephants wanted trade.

paragraphs.context: Some things never change. Inside the Eel, time stood still.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Lazy Eel winesink: a timeless, filthy tavern where candles give more smoke than light and the wine looks brown — 'Some things never change.'
paragraphs.simple: Davos goes to a dirty old tavern. The candles make more smoke than light, and the wine looks brown.

paragraphs.context: Before long, he found himself staring at the hearth. The
paragraphs.mainIdea: Davos's trauma: staring into the fire he sees only the past — burning ships, the wildfire chain — and wonders why the gods took his four sons but spared him.
paragraphs.simple: Looking at the fire, Davos remembers the battle where four of his sons died. He asks why the gods saved him and not them.

paragraphs.context: “Sweetness cloys. Tart fruit and tart women give life its
paragraphs.mainIdea: Xaro's famous line: 'Sweetness cloys. Tart fruit and tart women give life its savor' — flattery wrapped in a warning that Dany is too soft.
paragraphs.simple: Xaro says too much sweetness is sickening; sour things make life interesting — and hints Dany is too sweet and soft.

paragraphs.context: “There you see Astapor, and Yunkai, and Meereen.” Xaro pointed
paragraphs.mainIdea: Xaro's map lesson: Dany 'turned north when she should have continued south and west' — with his ships she could sail straight for Westeros and home.
paragraphs.simple: Xaro shows Dany a map: she went the wrong way. With his ships she can sail west to Westeros.

paragraphs.context: this is just some test to make sure that I love him
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jeyne is so broken by Ramsay's abuse that she thinks her rescuers are part of another cruel test, and begs them to tell him she loves him and will obey.
paragraphs.simple: She is terrified that this rescue is one of Ramsay's tricks to test her love. She promises she will do anything he wants, with him or with his dog, if only he will not cut off her feet. She swears she will never try to run away, and that she will give him sons.

paragraphs.context: The two we killed were just some miller’s sons
paragraphs.mainIdea: Theon admits he ordered the murder of two innocent miller's boys to cover up his failure to kill Bran and Rickon, and that his torture has left him unable to ever enjoy life again.
paragraphs.simple: When Rowan says the Stark boys were never his brothers, Theon agrees, but what he really means is different. He never hurt Bran or Rickon at all. The two boys who died were just a miller's sons, killed to hide his lie. He tries not to think about their mother, a woman he once knew and slept with. He remembers her body and her laugh, and knows that after what Ramsay did to him, he will never know such pleasures again.

paragraphs.context: She gave a hysterical laugh. “Frenya has the rope.”
paragraphs.mainIdea: Their escape plan collapses: the rope they need to climb down the wall is with Frenya, who stayed behind, and Holly is shot dead by crossbowmen.
paragraphs.simple: Their plan falls apart. Holly realizes the rope they need to get off the wall is with Frenya, who stayed behind at the drawbridge to hold off the guards. Then a crossbow bolt strikes Holly in the stomach, and a second one strikes her chest. She falls and dies in the snow.

paragraphs.context: Those bearers were slaves before I came. I made them free.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Dany sees that freeing the slaves changed little in practice: the freed bearers still carry the same heavy palanquin.
paragraphs.simple: She watches the Brazen Beasts help the fallen bearer. She thinks about how these men were slaves before she came to Meereen, carrying litters like this one. She made them free, yet the palanquin they carry is no lighter than before.

paragraphs.context: If I run from him, he will burn me and devour me.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Dany realizes she cannot outrun Drogon: if she flees, he will kill her. Her only chance is to stand her ground and show no fear.
paragraphs.simple: She looks into the dragon's molten eyes and feels she is looking into hell, but she forces herself not to look away. She has never been so sure of anything: if she runs, he will burn her and eat her. She must not run.

paragraphs.context: He is fire made flesh, she thought, and so am I.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Dany tames Drogon the way she once tamed horses, with a whip, commands, and no fear, and realizes she and the dragon are made of the same fire.
paragraphs.simple: She strikes the dragon with the whip, screaming “No!” again and again, until the great beast folds his wings and lies flat on his belly. He is wounded and bleeding. As she looks at him, she thinks: he is fire made into flesh, and so is she.

paragraphs.context: I am the guard who opened the gates and let the foe march through.
paragraphs.mainIdea: As Jon seals the bargain with Tormund, he adds his own bitter line to the Night's Watch oath: he is letting the ancient enemy through the Wall, and cannot turn back.
paragraphs.simple: Jon takes Tormund's hand to seal their deal. The words of his Night's Watch oath run through his mind, and he adds a new line of his own: he is the guard who opened the gates and let the enemy march through. He wishes he could know he is doing the right thing, but it is too late to turn back.

paragraphs.context: before we ever knew he’d died he rose pale with them blue eyes
paragraphs.mainIdea: Tormund tells Jon how he lost two sons: Dormund died in battle, and Torwynd died of cold, then rose as a wight, and Tormund had to kill his own son himself.
paragraphs.simple: Tormund's smile fades. He has lost two sons. Dormund was cut down in the battle for the Wall, still half a boy, by one of Stannis's knights. Torwynd, always sickly, died of cold one night, and before anyone knew he was dead, he rose again with pale blue eyes, as one of the dead. Tormund had to kill him himself. That was the hardest thing, he says, with tears in his eyes.

paragraphs.context: what are these wildlings, if not men
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jon turns the oath back on Marsh: the vow says “the shield that guards the realms of men”, and the wildlings are men too, so the oath demands protecting them.
paragraphs.simple: Jon asks Marsh whether he has forgotten the parts of the oath about the king and his lands. No one answers. Then Jon quotes the real words: “I am the shield that guards the realms of men.” And he asks: the wildlings, what are they, if not men? Marsh cannot answer.

paragraphs.context: They treated her promises as they did her threats.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Cersei lists every weapon she tried on her jailers, threats, commands, pleas, charm, bribes, and every one failed completely.
paragraphs.simple: She tried everything on the three septas. She threatened them, but they ignored her. She commanded them, but they disobeyed. She begged for a woman's pity, but they showed none. She tried being sweet and gentle, but they were not moved. She offered gold, honors, and pardons, and they treated her promises exactly the way they treated her threats: as nothing.

paragraphs.context: Safer to confess too much than too little.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Cersei's confession is a calculated move: she admits only the lesser sin of adultery, which her accusers already confessed to, hoping to avoid trial on the capital charges of treason and murder.
paragraphs.simple: Her confession is a plan, not true repentance. She admits she slept with Lancel and the Kettleblacks, but only because those men have already confessed, so denying it would be useless. She confesses to the smaller sins to try to escape the greater charges: treason and murder. She even adds the Kettleblack brothers, in case they talk. Safer to confess too much than too little.

paragraphs.context: Duskendale had been his finest hour, yet the memory tasted bitter on his tongue.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Barristan's proudest deed, rescuing the mad King Aerys from Duskendale, may have doomed the realm: had Aerys died there, Rhaegar would have become king instead.
paragraphs.simple: He remembers the things he saw serving Aerys, and wonders how much blood is on his own hands. If he had not rescued Aerys from Lord Darklyn's dungeons at Duskendale, the king might have died when Tywin sacked the town, and then Prince Rhaegar would have taken the throne, and perhaps healed the realm. Duskendale was his finest hour as a knight, yet the memory is bitter to him now.

paragraphs.context: She was returned to her father in the black of night, in nine pieces
paragraphs.mainIdea: Skahaz names the poisoner: Hizdahr's confectioner, forced to poison the locusts because the Sons of the Harpy held his nine-year-old daughter, whom they murdered and returned to him in nine pieces.
paragraphs.simple: Skahaz says he has caught the poisoner: Hizdahr's own confectioner. The man was only a tool. The Sons of the Harpy had taken his daughter and promised to return her alive once the queen was dead. Belwas ate the poisoned locusts instead and the dragon saved Dany, but no one saved the girl. She was returned to her father in the dark of night, cut into nine pieces, one for every year she had lived.

paragraphs.context: The Crow’s Eye fears you, my lord, why else send you so far away
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ralf the Limper voices what Victarion secretly fears: Euron sent him on this hopeless voyage because he is afraid of him, and never meant him to return.
paragraphs.simple: The Limper blames storms for the lost ships: three great storms, red winds from Valyria smelling of ash and brimstone, black winds driving them toward a cursed shore. He says the voyage was cursed from the start. Then he says what Victarion himself has thought: the Crow's Eye fears Victarion, and that is why he sent him so far away. Euron does not mean for any of them to return.

paragraphs.context: blind to the tentacles that grasp you at wrist and neck and ankle
paragraphs.mainIdea: Moqorro shows Victarion a vision of himself striding through flames with his bloody axe, blind to the tentacles and black strings that make him dance like a puppet.
paragraphs.simple: Moqorro says he has seen Victarion in his fires: striding through the flames, stern and fierce, his great axe dripping blood, but blind to the tentacles gripping his wrists, neck, and ankles, the black strings that make him dance. Victarion is angry: he was not made for dancing, and is no man's puppet.

paragraphs.context: to accompany their beloved master to the grave
paragraphs.mainIdea: Sweets explains with a ghastly laugh that dying masters “free” only their favorites, by slitting their throats so they can serve him in the afterlife. Sweets knows his own throat will be first.
paragraphs.simple: When Penny says some masters free their slaves when they die, Sweets laughs a horrible laugh. Only favorites are freed, he says, freed from the troubles of this world by having their throats cut, so they can follow their beloved master to the grave and serve him in the afterlife. Sweets would know: his throat will be the first one slit.

paragraphs.context: The last words he ever heard were, “A Lannister always pays his debts.”
paragraphs.mainIdea: Tyrion poisoned Nurse, the hated overseer, with mushroom soup, and his parting words were the Lannister saying: “A Lannister always pays his debts.”
paragraphs.simple: Tyrion tells Penny that sweet water did not save Nurse. The overseer died of the pale mare last night, or so everyone thinks. In truth, Tyrion nursed him and fed him wine, lemonsweet, and hot soup with slivers of mushroom in it: poison. The last word Nurse ever said was “No.” The last words he ever heard were Tyrion's: “A Lannister always pays his debts.”

paragraphs.context: But we never found the true horn, not for all our digging
paragraphs.mainIdea: Tormund reveals Mance's great threat was a bluff: the horn Melisandre burned was just a big horn from a giant's grave, the true Horn of Winter was never found.
paragraphs.simple: When Jon says Melisandre burned the Horn of Joramun, Tormund laughs. She burned a fine big horn, a thousand years old, found in a giant's grave, but it was never the true horn. Mance only wanted the crows to believe he could blow the Wall down. For all their digging, the wildlings never found the real Horn of Winter. If they had, Tormund jokes, every lord in the Seven Kingdoms would have chunks of Wall ice to cool his wine all summer.

paragraphs.context: Wildlings eating their own dead. Dead things in the woods.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Cotter Pyke's letter from Hardhome is a catalogue of horrors: ships lost, starving wildlings eating their own dead, and dead things in the woods and in the water.
paragraphs.simple: The letter from Hardhome says: six ships left, wild seas. The Blackbird lost with all hands. Two Lyseni ships driven aground. At Hardhome the wildlings are eating their own dead. There are dead things in the woods and dead things in the water. The Braavosi captains will only take women and children. The wildlings call them slavers. Send help by land, the seas are wracked by storms.

paragraphs.context: She wants fire, and Dorne sent her mud.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Barristan judges Quentyn's suit hopeless: Dany is a young girl who wants fire, passion and poetry, and Dorne sent her mud, a plain, dutiful, unexciting boy.
paragraphs.simple: Barristan thinks about why Quentyn never had a chance. Daenerys is still a young girl at heart, and she wants fire: passion, poetry, excitement. Dorne sent her mud. Quentyn is decent, sober, and dutiful, but not the sort to make a young girl's heart beat faster. Mud is useful, you can cool a fever with it, grow crops in it, feed children with it, while fire only burns you, but fools and children and young girls will choose fire every time.

paragraphs.context: “A boy,” he had proclaimed to the crowd. “A bold boy.”
paragraphs.mainIdea: Barristan recalls how he earned his name at ten: a vain boy who stole a horse and armor to joust as a mystery knight, unhorsed in one pass, and Prince Duncan named him “a bold boy.”
paragraphs.simple: He won the name “Barristan the Bold” when he was ten years old, a new-made squire so vain and foolish that he believed he could joust against proven knights. He borrowed a warhorse and armor from Lord Dondarrion and entered the lists at Blackhaven as a mystery knight. Even the herald laughed: his arms were so thin he could barely keep his lance point off the ground. Prince Duncan took pity on him, accepted his challenge, and unhorsed him in a single pass. Then the prince lifted off his helm and announced to the crowd: “A boy. A bold boy.” That was fifty-three years ago.

paragraphs.context: I had his foot cut off, roasted it up, and fed it to him
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Tattered Prince shows his ruthless humor: a deserter who blamed the bad food had his foot cut off, roasted, and fed to him, then was made the company cook, and the meals improved.
paragraphs.simple: The Tattered Prince says every deserter has an excuse. One charming boy said the other men made him do shameful things; he did not forgive him. Another said the company's food was so bad he had to flee before it made him sick, so the Prince had the man's foot cut off, roasted it, and fed it to him. Then he made the man the camp cook. The meals improved greatly, and when the man's contract ended he signed another one. Quentyn, though, has several of his best men locked in the queen's dungeons, and the Prince doubts Quentyn can even cook.

paragraphs.context: “What I want,” said the Tattered Prince, “is Pentos.”
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Tattered Prince names his true price for helping steal a dragon: not gold, but Pentos, his lost home city, which he wants back.
paragraphs.simple: Quentyn offers to double the Yunkish pay. The Tattered Prince laughs: double does not pay for dragons, and a man who pays in promises should promise more. When Quentyn offers to triple it, the Prince names his real price: Pentos itself, the city he came from and wants to rule again.

paragraphs.context: would not have bothered with a search. He would have burned that town
paragraphs.mainIdea: Myles Toyne tells Connington his failure at Stoney Sept: he wanted the glory of killing Robert himself, while Tywin would simply have burned the whole town, innocents and all, to be sure.
paragraphs.simple: Connington insisted no man could have done more than he did at Stoney Sept. Myles Toyne told him he was wrong: Lord Tywin would not have searched house by house. He would have burned the town and every living thing in it, men and boys, babes, knights, septons, pigs, whores, rats, rebels, and then sifted the ashes for Robert's bones. When Stark and Tully arrived, he would have pardoned them, and they would have gone home. Connington wanted the glory of slaying Robert in single combat, and did not want the name of butcher, so Robert escaped, and killed Rhaegar on the Trident.

paragraphs.context: abandon that same companion in a heartbeat if he were known to have greyscale
paragraphs.mainIdea: Connington hides his spreading greyscale: he soaks his blackening fingers in cheap wine each morning, knowing that men who would die for a comrade in battle would abandon him in a heartbeat if they knew.
paragraphs.simple: Each morning he orders the worst wine in the cellar, bars his door, and soaks his hand in it, a secret treatment for greyscale, since asking for vinegar would give him away. The nails of four fingers are black now, and the grey is creeping up past the knuckle of his middle finger. He thinks of cutting the fingers off, but how would he explain that? He dares not let anyone know. Strange as it seems, men who would gladly risk death in battle to save a comrade would abandon that same comrade in a heartbeat if they learned he had greyscale.

paragraphs.context: The four were not the first to taste human flesh during this grim march
paragraphs.mainIdea: Asha is horrified but not surprised: four men were caught butchering a corpse for food, and she wagers they were not the first cannibals on this march, only the first caught.
paragraphs.simple: Asha was as horrified as everyone when Aly Mormont told her that four of Peasebury's men had been found cutting up one of the late Lord Fell's men, carving flesh from his thighs while his forearm roasted on a spit. But she could not pretend to be surprised. She would wager these four were not the first to taste human flesh on this grim, starving march, only the first to be discovered.

paragraphs.context: it was the only part of a woman they valued
paragraphs.mainIdea: Asha reflects on Suggs's favorite insult: it is strange that men like him use that word to degrade women, when it names the only part of a woman they value.
paragraphs.simple: Suggs calls her that word again. Asha thinks it is strange: men like Suggs use that word to put women down, when it is the only part of a woman they actually value. And Suggs is worse than others who say it: when he says the word, he means every bit of its cruelty.

paragraphs.context: My name is Theon. You have to know your name.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The broken prisoner is Theon, Asha's brother, unrecognizable, and his one anchor to sanity is repeating his own name: you have to know your name.
paragraphs.simple: The old man raises his eyes: “Sister. See. This time I knew you.” Asha's heart skips: “Theon?” His lips pull back in what might be a grin, half his teeth gone, the rest broken. He repeats his name like a lesson: “Theon. My name is Theon. You have to know your name.”

paragraphs.context: With this gift of innocence and beauty, we honor both the gods
paragraphs.mainIdea: Victarion “honors” the seven loveliest captive girls by setting them adrift in a burning ship, a sacrifice to both his gods, to buy fair winds.
paragraphs.simple: After his speech, Victarion has the seven girls he claimed, the loveliest found aboard the Willing Maiden, brought on deck. He kisses each on the cheek and tells them of the honor awaiting them, though they cannot understand his words. Then he puts them aboard a captured fishing boat, cuts it loose, and sets it on fire. As the fleet rows past the burning boat, he proclaims: “With this gift of innocence and beauty, we honor both the gods.” He prays they will be reborn in light, pure and untouched, or else feast and dance in the Drowned God's halls until the seas dry up. It seems to him their cries turn to joyful song, and a great wind rises to fill the sails.

paragraphs.context: ‘No mortal man shall sound me and live.’
paragraphs.mainIdea: Moqorro reads the horn's glyphs: it is named Dragonbinder; no mortal who sounds it can live, but whoever blows it matters not, for the dragons come to the horn's master, claimed with blood.
paragraphs.simple: Moqorro reads the strange letters on the horn's golden bands. One band names the horn: “I am Dragonbinder.” Another says: “No mortal man shall sound me and live”, the man who blew it at the kingsmoot died burned from within. But a third band says: “Blood for fire, fire for blood.” It does not matter who blows the horn; the dragons will come to the horn's master. Victarion must claim the horn, with blood.

paragraphs.context: A wager every captain hopes to lose.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The old man is an insurer: for a price he writes “binders” promising to pay a ship's value if it is lost, a wager every captain hopes to lose, since winning means losing his ship and maybe his life.
paragraphs.simple: The girl asks what the old man is selling. He writes each captain a “binder”: if their ship is lost in a storm or taken by pirates, he promises to pay them the value of the ship and everything in it. It is a kind of wager, a wager every captain hopes to lose. If they “win” the wager, they lose their ships, and often their lives. But a drowning captain can take some comfort knowing his widow and children will not go hungry.

paragraphs.context: she knew it wasn’t so. They were skins.
paragraphs.mainIdea: In the vault beneath the temple, Arya sees a thousand faces hanging on the walls, and realizes they are not masks but the flayed skins of the dead.
paragraphs.simple: The kindly man leads her deep below the temple, to a chamber where a thousand faces hang on the walls, old and young, pale and dark, smiling and frowning, men, women, and babes. She tells herself they are only masks. But even as she thinks it, she knows it is not so. They are skins, the faces cut from the dead.

paragraphs.context: on the day Lord Eddard Stark had lost his head
paragraphs.mainIdea: Standing on the sept steps, Cersei remembers she stood in this very spot when Ned Stark was beheaded, a death Joffrey ordered against the plan, after which there was no turning back.
paragraphs.simple: On the marble steps of the sept, it suddenly comes to her: she has stood in this very spot before, on the day Lord Eddard Stark lost his head. That was not supposed to happen. Joffrey was supposed to spare him and send him to the Wall, with Sansa kept at court as hostage. Ned had swallowed his honor and confessed to treason to save his daughter. But Joffrey commanded his head be struck off instead, and Janos Slynt lifted it by the hair as the blood flowed down the steps. After that, there was no turning back.

paragraphs.context: The queen began to see familiar faces
paragraphs.mainIdea: As she walks, Cersei's mind breaks: she hallucinates the dead, Tywin's frown, Melara's accusing eyes, Ned Stark, Sansa, Tyrion jeering, and Joffrey, in the faces of the crowd.
paragraphs.simple: The queen begins to see familiar faces in the crowd. A bald man with bushy whiskers frowns down with her father's frown, so like Lord Tywin that she stumbles. A girl beneath a fountain stares at her with Melara Hetherspoon's accusing eyes. She sees Ned Stark, and little Sansa with her auburn hair beside him. Every child in the crowd becomes her brother Tyrion, jeering at her as he jeered when Joffrey died. And there is Joffrey too, her firstborn, her beautiful bright boy with golden curls and a sweet smile.

paragraphs.context: to cast you down and take all you hold most dear
paragraphs.mainIdea: In the crowd Cersei sees the hag from her childhood, Maggy the Frog, hissing her old prophecy: another queen, younger and more beautiful, will cast her down and take all she holds dear.
paragraphs.simple: Suddenly the hag is there in the crowd, the fortune-teller from her childhood, with sagging breasts and warty green skin, leering with malice shining from her yellow eyes. Cersei hears her hiss the old prophecy: “Queen you shall be, until there comes another, younger and more beautiful, to cast you down and take all you hold most dear.” And then Cersei cannot hold back her tears any longer.

paragraphs.context: There has never been a slave who did not choose to be a slave
paragraphs.mainIdea: Tyrion's bleak philosophy: every slave chooses slavery, the choice may be between bondage and death, but the choice is always there; Penny, he sees, has been searching for a new master since her brother died.
paragraphs.simple: Penny says it wasn't so bad with Yezzan. Tyrion thinks she is not entirely wrong: Yezzan's slaves ate better than many peasants, and most masters treat their slaves decently, the way men treat their dogs and horses. Proud men shout they would rather die free than live as slaves, but when it comes to it, such men are rare as dragon's teeth, or the world would not be so full of slaves. There has never been a slave who did not choose to be a slave, he thinks. The choice may be between bondage and death, but the choice is always there. And Penny, he realizes, has been searching for a new master ever since her brother Groat lost his head: she wants someone to take care of her and tell her what to do.

paragraphs.context: The mummer show is over. Fight or hide or shit yourself, as you like
paragraphs.mainIdea: Tyrion slaps Penny awake from her dream of her dead brother: the performing days are over, Crunch is dead, and she must put on armor, fight, hide, or panic, but do it in steel.
paragraphs.simple: Penny is about to cry, telling Tyrion her dream: her brother alive again, the two of them jousting before a great lord on their pig and dog, men throwing roses, both so happy. Tyrion slaps her, a soft blow, barely a flick of the wrist, leaving no mark, but her eyes fill with tears. “If you want to dream, go back to sleep,” he tells her. “When you wake, we will still be escaped slaves in the middle of a siege. Crunch is dead, and the pig too, most likely. Find some armor and put it on, no matter where it pinches. The mummer show is over. Fight or hide or soil yourself, as you like, but whatever you do, you will do it wearing steel.”

paragraphs.context: the bloody bodies up in crimson cloaks, a gift for the new king
paragraphs.mainIdea: Barristan tells the Shavepate that Tywin murdered Rhaegar's two children and wrapped their bodies in Lannister crimson cloaks as a gift for Robert.
paragraphs.simple: Barristan explains to Skahaz why he will not allow the murder of children. When Tywin Lannister took King's Landing, his men killed Prince Rhaegar's two children: little Rhaenys and baby Aegon. Tywin had their bloody bodies wrapped in crimson Lannister cloaks and presented them to the new king, Robert, as a gift. Barristan was wounded on the Trident and never saw it, but he often wonders: if he had seen Robert smile over the ruined bodies of Rhaegar's children, no army could have stopped him from killing Robert.

paragraphs.context: She died never knowing that Ser Barristan had loved her.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Barristan's great unspoken love: he secretly loved Ashara Dayne all his life, but as a Kingsguard sworn to celibacy he never told her, and she died without knowing.
paragraphs.simple: Barristan thinks of Ashara Dayne, the lady he loved in secret. Her daughter was stillborn, and Ashara threw herself from a tower in grief, perhaps also grieving for the man who dishonored her at Harrenhal. She died never knowing that Ser Barristan had loved her. He was a knight of the Kingsguard, sworn to have no wife or love, so telling her could have done no good. But silence did no good either. He wonders: if he had unhorsed Rhaegar at Harrenhal and crowned Ashara queen of love and beauty, might she have chosen him instead of Stark?

paragraphs.context: I want Cletus and Will and Maester Kedry to be alive again.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Burned and dying, Quentyn drops the heroic talk: what he truly wants is not dragons or glory but his dead friends alive again and an ordinary happy life.
paragraphs.simple: As Quentyn lies dying, he stops pretending. He did not want to die at all. What he really wants is to go back to Yronwood, kiss his sisters, marry Gwyneth, have a child, ride in tourneys, hawk and hunt, visit his mother in Norvos, read his father's books. He wants Cletus and Will and Maester Kedry, his dead companions, to be alive again. He never wanted Daenerys to hear he had bedded some whore; he only wanted to come home a man grown, proven in battle, and make his father proud.

paragraphs.context: He wants his mother and does not understand why she’s not here.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Quentyn realizes too late that the dragon Viserion is not attacking but searching: sniffing the intruders for Daenerys, his mother, confused that she is not there.
paragraphs.simple: The dragon Viserion comes down between the Dornishmen and the door with a roar. His head moves side to side as he inspects the intruders, sniffing them, and stares longest at Pretty Meris. Quentyn suddenly understands: the dragon knows she is female. He is looking for Daenerys. He wants his mother and does not understand why she is not here. Then the dragon's head turns, and Quentyn has time to say a prayer before the white fire washes over him.

paragraphs.context: I will cut out your bastard’s heart and eat it
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ramsay Bolton's letter demands Jon hand over Stannis's wife, daughter, Melisandre, Val, the wildling babe, and Reek, threatening to cut out Jon's heart and eat it if he refuses.
paragraphs.simple: Jon reads Ramsay's letter to the castle. Ramsay calls himself trueborn Lord of Winterfell now. He demands his bride back, the false king's queen, his daughter, his red witch, his wildling princess, the wildling babe, and his Reek. Send them to him, bastard, and he will not trouble Jon or his black crows. Keep them from him, and he will cut out Jon's bastard heart and eat it. Jon decides to march on Ramsay himself, and asks the wildlings to come with him.

paragraphs.context: He never felt the fourth knife. Only the cold
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jon is stabbed by his own men in the mutiny at Castle Black: after the third dagger he falls, and the fourth knife he never feels, only the cold.
paragraphs.simple: After Jon announces he will march on Winterfell, Wick Whittlestick grabs his arm and says “Lord Commander” in an accusing voice. Jon hears the whisper of steel and feels a dagger between his shoulder blades; he spins and finds Wick with a bloody blade. Words he never remembers speaking come out: “Ghost.” Then Bowen Marsh is there weeping, and Jon is stabbed again. He falls to his knees, pulls a dagger free, and whispers “Ghost.” When the third dagger takes him between the shoulder blades, he falls face-first into the snow. He never feels the fourth knife. Only the cold.

paragraphs.context: Quentyn was here for dragons, not Daenerys.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Barristan sees through the Dornish story: Quentyn never loved Daenerys; duty, honor, and thirst for glory brought him, and what Dorne truly wanted was dragons.
paragraphs.simple: The Dornishmen claim Quentyn loved Daenerys. Barristan has heard enough. He has spent his life around kings and queens and princes, and he knows Sunspear means to take up arms against the Iron Throne. Doran Martell would not call his spears without hope of victory. Duty brought Prince Quentyn here: duty, honor, thirst for glory, never love. Quentyn was here for dragons, not Daenerys. And now the boy is dead, and Barristan must tell his father.

paragraphs.context: “Not stones.” The old woman’s voice was full of grief, of fear. “Corpses.”
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Yunkai'i are not hurling stones from their trebuchets but corpses, dead bodies meant to spread disease and terror inside Meereen.
paragraphs.simple: Barristan watches the Yunkish trebuchets at work and asks what they are throwing. An old woman answers, her voice full of grief and fear: “Not stones. Corpses.” The Yunkai'i are flinging dead bodies over the walls of Meereen, a plague weapon meant to sicken and terrify the city. Barristan orders his own trebuchets to answer, and the siege of Meereen begins in earnest.

paragraphs.context: To go forward, you must go back.
paragraphs.mainIdea: In a fever dream, Quaithe's riddle returns to Dany: to go north you must journey south, to go forward you must go back, to touch the light you must pass beneath the shadow.
paragraphs.simple: Sick and starving in the Dothraki sea, Dany dreams. All her cares and pains fall away, and she seems to float upward, flying once again, spinning and laughing as the stars wheel around her and whisper secrets. She hears Quaithe's voice: “To go north, you must journey south. To reach the west, you must go east. To go forward, you must go back. To touch the light you must pass beneath the shadow.” When she wakes, she decides: to go forward she must go back, back to Meereen, and she calls Drogon to carry her.

paragraphs.context: Dragons plant no trees. Remember that.
paragraphs.mainIdea: In her fever dream, a voice like Ser Jorah's warns Dany: dragons plant no trees, meaning destroyers do not build; she must remember who she is and what she was made to be.
paragraphs.simple: In her dream Dany hears a whisper that sounds like Ser Jorah, growing fainter as if he is falling behind: “You are the blood of the dragon. Dragons plant no trees. Remember that. Remember who you are, what you were made to be. Remember your words.” The meaning is that dragons, and Targaryens, are destroyers, not builders: they burn and conquer, they do not plant trees for the future. Dany takes it as a command to stop trying to be a peacemaker and be the dragon instead.

paragraphs.context: “Winter,” said Ser Kevan. The word made a white mist in the air.
paragraphs.mainIdea: A white raven arrives from the Citadel, the formal announcement that winter has come at last, and Kevan speaks the word into the freezing air.
paragraphs.simple: A white raven has come from the Citadel. White ravens are only sent to announce the changing of a season, and this one brings the news everyone has dreaded: winter has come. Ser Kevan stands at the window and says the word aloud: “Winter.” His breath makes a white mist in the cold air. He turns away from the window to face the small council, where Pycelle is prattling about the cold and the price of grain.

paragraphs.context: kingship is his duty, that a king must put his people first
paragraphs.mainIdea: Varys explains why Aegon will be a better king than Tommen: raised among common folk and trained in every hardship, he believes kingship is duty to the people, not a birthright.
paragraphs.simple: Varys tells the dying Kevan why he serves Aegon. The boy has been shaped for rule since before he could walk: trained in arms, taught to read and write, to speak several tongues, to study history, law, and poetry. But more than that, he has lived with fisherfolk, worked with his hands, swum in rivers, mended nets, washed his own clothes, fished, cooked, and bound up wounds. He knows what it is like to be hungry, hunted, and afraid. Tommen has been taught that kingship is his right. Aegon knows that kingship is his duty, that a king must put his people first, and live and rule for them.

paragraphs.context: yet even in those days we were few.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Leaf tells Bran that her people, the children of the forest, are dying out.
paragraphs.simple: Before men came to Westeros, the land belonged to Leaf's people, the children of the forest. But they were always few, because the gods gave them long lives and small numbers. Now their time is ending. The giants, lions, unicorns, and mammoths are almost gone, and one day the direwolves will go as well.

paragraphs.context: For men, time is a river.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Brynden teaches Bran that trees and men feel time in different ways.
paragraphs.simple: For men, time is a river: we are carried from the past to the present and can never go back. Trees do not move. They grow and die in one place, so time does not carry them along. To a weirwood, a thousand years feels like a single moment.

paragraphs.context: past, present, and future are one.
paragraphs.mainIdea: A trained greenseer can see the past through the weirwoods, because to them past, present, and future are one.
paragraphs.simple: Men live only in the now. The past is misty memory, and the future is dark. Trees live far longer than men, and to them seasons pass like the beat of a moth's wing. Past, present, and future are one. Once Bran masters his gift, he can see what the trees saw long ago.

paragraphs.context: in nests of weirwood roots that wove under and through and around their bodies.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Deep in the caves, old singers sit half-dead in nests of weirwood roots, watching Bran pass.
paragraphs.simple: As Hodor, Bran explores the caves and finds a chamber full of singers. They sit like kings in nests of weirwood roots that grow under, through, and around their bodies. Most look dead, but their eyes open and follow his torch, and one tries to speak.

paragraphs.context: find a better match for her than Ramsay Snow.
paragraphs.mainIdea: This is Stannis's letter: he is marching on Winterfell to save Jon's 'sister' and stop Roose Bolton.
paragraphs.simple: This is a letter from Stannis Baratheon. His army has grown to five thousand men. Roose Bolton is marching on Winterfell to wed his bastard son to Jon's half sister. Stannis will march against Bolton and try to save the girl. Jon and his brothers must hold the Wall until he returns.

paragraphs.context: And of me. Stannis would have taken it for treason.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jon has secretly swapped the babies: Mance's son (Dalla's boy) is hidden, and Gilly's 'monster' took his place, so Melisandre cannot burn the king's blood.
paragraphs.simple: Jon swapped the two babies. Dalla's boy is Mance Rayder's son, and his king's blood would interest Melisandre. Gilly's baby, called Monster, was sent away in his place. Jon fears that if Melisandre learns the truth, she will take the boy, and Stannis will call it treason.

paragraphs.context: Was Plumm the third treason, or the second?
paragraphs.mainIdea: Dany remembers the prophecy of three treasons and wonders who will betray her — Jorah? Brown Ben?
paragraphs.simple: In the House of the Undying, Dany was told: 'Three treasons will you know.' Now she wonders about the men around her. Is Brown Ben Plumm a treason for gold or blood? And what about Ser Jorah, her gruff old bear — can she trust him? She feels she can trust no one.

paragraphs.context: Daenerys dare not open her gates to let them in.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Dany cannot help the sick Astapori: opening the gates would bring the plague inside, and even her healers are dying.
paragraphs.simple: Thousands of sick Astapori wait outside Meereen's walls, but Dany dare not let them in. She sent healers, but some of them sickened too, and nothing slowed the plague. Even separating the healthy from the sick failed: within days, the healthy were sick as well.

paragraphs.context: putting mine own face on their lie.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Theon knows Bolton is only using him to make the false Arya's wedding look real; afterward he will be given back to Ramsay.
paragraphs.simple: Roose Bolton dressed Theon as a lord again so the wedding of the false Arya will look true. Theon is a mask on Bolton's lie. Once she is wedded and bedded, Bolton will have no more use for him. Theon knows he will be handed back to Ramsay, who will turn him into Reek again.

paragraphs.context: True to his word, he showed them mercy and did not flay a one.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Bolton's 'mercy' is a cruel joke: the workers rebuilt Winterfell, and then he hanged them all.
paragraphs.simple: When Bolton took Winterfell, his men hanged the boldest squatters and put the rest to work rebuilding. Bolton had promised mercy to those who served well. When the work was done, he kept his word in his own way: he hanged the workers too, and only spared them the flaying.

paragraphs.context: He was kind to me, but never warm.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Theon remembers he was never truly a Stark: he was Ned's hostage, and kindness never meant safety.
