paragraphs.simple: Theon thinks back on his years at Winterfell. He was not a son of the house; he was a hostage, kept to ensure his father's good behavior. Ned Stark was kind to him, but never warm. Theon always knew that one day Ned might have to put him to death.

paragraphs.context: The eyes of the bride were brown. Big and brown and full of fear.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Winterfell has turned grey and dead, and the frightened 'bride' looks to broken Theon for a rescue he cannot give.
paragraphs.simple: All color has drained from Winterfell: grey walls, grey sky, grey snow. The only living color is the brown eyes of the bride, wide with fear. She looks to Theon for rescue, as if he were a hero from a story. But he cannot even help himself.

paragraphs.context: it was her marriage that made Dorne part of the Seven Kingdoms.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Doran tells the history of the Water Gardens: the first Daenerys's marriage brought Dorne into the Seven Kingdoms.
paragraphs.simple: An ancestor of Doran built the Water Gardens for his Targaryen bride, a princess named Daenerys. She was sister to King Daeron the Good. Her marriage is what made Dorne part of the Seven Kingdoms — even though she truly loved the king's bastard brother, Daemon Blackfyre.

paragraphs.context: Be careful, though. King’s Landing is a pit of snakes.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Doran lays out his secret plan: use Balon Swann, send Nymeria to King's Landing as Dorne's eyes, and never defy the throne openly — yet.
paragraphs.simple: Doran will not harm Ser Balon Swann, who ate his bread and salt. He will send him after Darkstar with Obara, and send Nymeria to King's Landing. Dorne needs a voice in council and an ear at court. But Dorne must not openly defy the Iron Throne yet.

paragraphs.context: Daenerys will execute me and pardon you, but the reverse is just as likely.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Tyrion exposes Jorah: he was Varys's spy, Dany cast him out, and now he hopes to buy a pardon by delivering Tyrion.
paragraphs.simple: Tyrion sees through Jorah at last. He was not on the queen's business — he was running. Dany sent him away because he had been spying on her. Now he hopes to win her favor back by handing her Tyrion. But Dany may just as well execute Jorah and pardon Tyrion instead.

paragraphs.context: the muttering about how dwarf luck had failed them.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The ship lies becalmed, and the frightened crew blames the dwarfs for the lost wind.
paragraphs.simple: For twelve days the ship has floated without wind in the Gulf of Grief. The crew grows ugly in mood, and they whisper that dwarf luck has failed them. The cook still rubs Tyrion's head for luck, hoping to stir a wind, but the rest give him venomous looks.

paragraphs.context: He never cut me without cause.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Broken by Ramsay, Theon now blames the victim — even telling the abused 'bride' that Ramsay only hurts them when they deserve it.
paragraphs.simple: Ramsay makes Theon serve as his wife's bath maid. The girl is covered in bruises, but Theon tells her it is her own fault for not pleasing Ramsay. He even says Ramsay never cut him without cause. Theon has come to believe his tormentor's cruelty is deserved.

paragraphs.context: Lord Winter has joined us with his levies,
paragraphs.mainIdea: A sentry jokes that winter itself has joined their side — then sees Theon's face and spits.
paragraphs.simple: Snow covers everything. In the yard, Ryswells and Barrowton boys fight with snowballs, while squires arm snowmen with spears and shields along the walls. A sentry jokes that 'Lord Winter has joined us with his levies.' Then he sees Theon's face, remembers who he is talking to, and spits.

paragraphs.context: Brandon was fostered at Barrowton with old Lord Dustin
paragraphs.mainIdea: Lady Dustin tells Theon she loved Brandon Stark — Ned's wild older brother — and she is no friend of the Boltons.
paragraphs.simple: Lady Dustin remembers Brandon Stark, Ned's older brother. He was fostered at Barrowton and spent his youth riding. Her father hoped to marry her to a Stark, and she loved Brandon. She is old now, but she still honors his memory — and she is no friend of the Boltons.

paragraphs.context: putting her in the Seastone Chair on Pyke and ruling through her,
paragraphs.mainIdea: Asha sees through Ser Justin Massey: he wants to marry her so he can rule the Iron Islands through her.
paragraphs.simple: Asha knows what Justin Massey wants. He lost his own lands, so he needs a rich marriage. Stannis stopped him wedding the wildling princess, so now he aims at Asha. He dreams of seating her on the Seastone Chair and ruling the Iron Islands through her.

paragraphs.context: the queen they followed was the red one at Castle Black,
paragraphs.mainIdea: 'Queen's men' follow Melisandre, the red woman — not Stannis's true queen.
paragraphs.simple: Asha watches the king's soldiers pray to the Lord of Light. The other men call them 'queen's men.' But the queen they follow is not Stannis's wife, left behind at Eastwatch. It is the red woman at Castle Black — Melisandre.

paragraphs.context: her worth as a hostage was less than naught.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Asha knows she is a worthless hostage: Euron would never ransom her, and Stannis cannot understand a woman like her.
paragraphs.simple: Asha thinks Stannis a fool to value her as a prisoner. Her uncle Euron rules the Iron Islands now and would not care if she lived or died. Her husband could never pay a ransom either. And Stannis finds armed women like her strange and unfathomable.

paragraphs.context: my brother Viserys is to take Prince Doran’s daughter Arianne for his queen.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The secret pact: Dorne promised to help overthrow Robert, and Viserys was to marry Arianne Martell.
paragraphs.simple: Dany reads out the secret pact, signed in Braavos when she was a little girl. Ser Willem Darry signed for her family; Prince Oberyn signed for Dorne. In return for Dorne's help overthrowing the Usurper, her brother Viserys was to take Prince Doran's daughter Arianne for his queen.

paragraphs.context: frogs who turn into enchanted princes when kissed by their true love.
paragraphs.mainIdea: 'Frog' is Quentyn Martell, a Dornish prince — and Dany teases him with the fairy tale.
paragraphs.simple: The squire called Frog is really Prince Quentyn Martell of Dorne. Dany explains the joke: in Westerosi children's tales, frogs turn into enchanted princes when kissed by their true love. Smiling, she asks him: 'Tell me, Prince Quentyn, are you enchanted?'

paragraphs.context: new princes sprang up from nowhere and took their thrones.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Iron Bank does not forgive debts — it replaces the rulers who owe it.
paragraphs.simple: Tycho Nestoris seems cultured and courteous, but his bank is fearsome. When princes failed to pay lesser banks, the bankers were ruined. When princes failed to repay the Iron Bank, new princes sprang up from nowhere and took their thrones. Jon's loan may cost him dearly.

paragraphs.context: a slave praying not for his own death but for his master
paragraphs.mainIdea: The kindly man tells how the Faceless Men began: a slave prayed for his master's death and paid with his own life of service.
paragraphs.simple: At first, the Faceless Men gave death only to those who yearned for it. Then a slave prayed for his master's death instead, offering all he had. The first brother granted it — but a slave owns nothing but his life, so the price was his lifelong service. From that moment, they were two.

paragraphs.context: the girl was just a mummer’s ploy, a lamb in a direwolf’s skin.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Theon sees Roose's cold plan: send the untrustworthy northmen out to die against Stannis before the fake-Arya lie collapses.
paragraphs.simple: Theon reads Roose Bolton's mind. The castle cannot hold out long, and the northern lords may not be loyal. Only the false Arya holds them here — a lamb in a direwolf's skin. So why not send the northmen to fight Stannis before the lie is exposed? Every fallen man is one less enemy.

paragraphs.context: he would pull out your entrails and make you eat them,
paragraphs.mainIdea: Lady Dustin warns the Freys: the northern lords lost kin at the Red Wedding and hate them.
paragraphs.simple: Lady Dustin tells the Freys to be careful. Lord Wyman Manderly is not the only northman who lost kin at the Red Wedding. Whoresbane Umber, the Flints, Cerwyns, Tallharts, and others all had men with the Young Wolf. They hate the Freys — only fear keeps them in check.

paragraphs.context: so near and yet so distant. The poor wretch had returned too late.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Tyrion reads Jorah's face: he returned too late — Daenerys has married another.
paragraphs.simple: Jorah stares at Meereen, and Tyrion reads his look easily: so near, and yet so distant. The poor wretch has returned too late. The guards say Daenerys is wed to a Meereenese slaver, though some slaves insist it is a lie and call her Mhysa — Mother.

paragraphs.context: men remember the wrongs done to their forebears, no peace will ever last.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Tytos Blackwood explains why the Bracken feud never ends: old wrongs are never forgotten.
paragraphs.simple: The Brackens and Blackwoods have made a hundred peaces, many sealed with marriages. There is Blackwood blood in every Bracken and Bracken blood in every Blackwood. But each time some new quarrel breaks out, the old wounds bleed again. So long as men remember the wrongs done to their forebears, no peace will ever last.

paragraphs.context: When a man takes the black, his crimes are wiped away.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jon offers Cregan Karstark the Night's Watch: taking the black wipes away his crimes.
paragraphs.simple: Jon tells Cregan Karstark his choice is death or the black. Stannis will have him executed when he returns — unless he wears a black cloak. When a man takes the black, his crimes are wiped away. Even a man like Cregan can start again.

paragraphs.context: what good did it do him?
paragraphs.mainIdea: Brown Ben explains the sellsword's creed: the bold ones don't live to grow old — his men simply didn't want to die.
paragraphs.simple: Brown Ben tells Dany why the Second Sons left her. He once found a dead man with a fortune in gold sewn into his coat — and what good did it do him? Dead men spend nothing. There are old sellswords and bold sellswords, but no old bold sellswords. His boys didn't care to die.

paragraphs.context: had made camp to the east, choking off the road to the Khyzai Pass.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Meereen is surrounded on every side: Yunkish tents, Ghiscari legions, and sellswords.
paragraphs.simple: Dany looks out over the siege. Yellow Yunkish tents stand in rows beside the sea. Two iron legions from New Ghis camp across the river to the north; two more Ghiscari legions camp to the east, choking the road to the Khyzai Pass. The free companies' horse lines and cookfires lie to the south.

sentences.context: “Who is this man? He is no king of mine.”
sentences.simple: The clansmen would reject Stannis: to them, a king who only gives orders would not be a true king.
sentences.grammar: Quoted speech imagining what the clansmen would say to one another. Jon’s point: command them, and they will deny that you are their king.

sentences.context: All ruined, all desolate, all fallen.
sentences.simple: The whole city was ruined, empty, and fallen.
sentences.grammar: Three bare phrases with no verb, piled up for force. Each repeats the same idea — everything is destroyed — and the pile-up makes the ruin feel total.

sentences.context: “When the year turns,” came the answer, “Nyessos and Malaquo go hand in hand, and the elephants show stripes.”
sentences.simple: When the new year comes, Nyessos and Malaquo will rule together as partners, and even the peace party will turn to war.
sentences.grammar: “Go hand in hand” means to act together as partners. The boatman’s news: the two triarchs will share power, and the elephants (the peace party) will “show stripes” — act like tigers, the war party.

sentences.context: “Words are wind,” said the young woman behind Lord Wyman’s high seat, the handsome one with the long brown braid.
sentences.simple: Promises mean nothing; they blow away like wind.
sentences.grammar: “Words are wind” is a common Westerosi saying: talk is empty and cannot be trusted. Here it dismisses Stannis’s claims as mere talk.

sentences.context: That is not Lord Eddard’s daughter.
sentences.simple: The girl Ramsay is to marry is not really Eddard Stark’s daughter — she is a fake.
sentences.grammar: A short, flat sentence of denial. Theon grew up with the Stark girls and can see at a glance that this “Arya” is an impostor.

sentences.context: So let us hope it never comes to that.
sentences.simple: So let us hope we never have to find out whose side they would fight on.
sentences.grammar: “Come to that” means “reach that situation.” Jon is saying: let us hope we never face the test Marsh describes — new recruits turning against the Watch.

sentences.context: “The best calumnies are spiced with truth,” suggested Qavo,
sentences.simple: The best lies are mixed with a little truth.
sentences.grammar: “Calumny” is a false, damaging story. “Spiced with” borrows from cooking: a lie spreads best when a true detail is mixed in, like spice in food.

sentences.context: Your grandsire commanded it. A woods witch had told him that the prince was promised would be born of their line.
sentences.simple: Your grandfather ordered the marriage because a woods witch told him that the promised prince would be born from Aerys and Rhaella’s children.
sentences.grammar: “The prince that was promised” is a prophecy known in Westeros. The sentence explains why Aerys and Rhaella married even though they did not love each other.

sentences.context: “You are fighting shadows when you should be fighting the men who cast them,” Daario went on.
sentences.simple: You are fighting imaginary enemies instead of the real men behind them.
sentences.grammar: “Fighting shadows” is a figure of speech: Daario means Dany is striking at nothing. The “men who cast them” are the Great Masters who create the danger.

sentences.context: Griff would be glad to go back to his own true colors too, though his once red hair had gone to grey.
sentences.simple: Griff also longs to stop hiding who he is — though his once-red hair has turned grey with age.
sentences.grammar: “True colors” means his real identity and appearance. The blue dye hides who he really is; the sentence hints that his disguise — and his patience with it — is wearing thin.

sentences.context: In the time it took the Windblown to ride three miles, the Yunkai’i had fallen two-and-a-half miles behind.
sentences.simple: While the Windblown rode three miles forward, the Yunkish army fell two and a half miles behind them — they are hopelessly slow.
sentences.grammar: A comic comparison of distances: the “mighty” Yunkish host cannot even keep up with its own sellswords. The joke is that they march backward while others march forward.

sentences.context: You are clinging to Sea Dragon Point the way a drowning man clings to a bit of wreckage.
sentences.simple: You are holding on to Sea Dragon Point as desperately as a drowning man holds on to floating wreckage.
sentences.grammar: A simile: Tris compares Asha’s grip on worthless land to a drowning man clutching debris. The point is that Sea Dragon Point cannot save her — it is only wreckage.

sentences.context: I am no lady, but even Vogarro’s whore knows the taste of falsehood.
sentences.simple: Even a lowly woman like me can tell when someone is lying.
sentences.grammar: She calls herself “Vogarro’s whore” with bitter pride: even someone at the bottom of society can taste a lie. It is a boast about her street wisdom, not humility.

sentences.context: “Your nightmare, my life.”
sentences.simple: What you dream about in fear is what I live through every day.
sentences.grammar: A dry, bleak joke in four words. Edd dreamed Jon was his steward; Jon answers that Edd’s nightmare is Jon’s actual daily life.

sentences.context: “Stannis burned the wrong man.”
sentences.simple: The man Stannis burned was not really Mance Rayder.
sentences.grammar: A flat statement hiding a huge secret: by Melisandre’s magic, the man who burned was the Lord of Bones wearing Mance’s shape — the real Mance lives.

sentences.context: “When treating with liars, even an honest man must lie.
sentences.simple: When you deal with liars, even an honest man has to lie too.
sentences.grammar: A general rule stated as wisdom: Manderly explains that his false cruelty was forced on him — survival among liars required deception.

sentences.context: Robett, bring the lad.
sentences.simple: Robett, bring the boy in.
sentences.grammar: A quiet command with enormous weight: Manderly is about to reveal a living Stark heir — the “price” he will ask of Stannis.

sentences.context: It is Eroeh all over again.
sentences.simple: This is just like what happened with Eroeh.
sentences.grammar: “All over again” means the same thing happening a second time. Dany means her attempt to save people has once more brought them ruin — as with the girl Eroeh, whom she “saved” only to doom.

sentences.context: “On what terms?” Beware the perfumed seneschal, Quaithe had said.
sentences.simple: “On what terms?” Dany remembers Quaithe’s warning: beware the perfumed seneschal.
sentences.grammar: A remembered warning from the masked woman Quaithe. The “perfumed seneschal” is Reznak mo Reznak — Dany is wondering whether Quaithe’s warning was about him.

sentences.context: You cannot help her, but he can.
sentences.simple: You cannot save your sister, but Mance can.
sentences.grammar: Melisandre tells Jon the painful truth and the offer together: Jon is bound by his vows, but the man beside them (Mance, in disguise) could go south and rescue the girl.

sentences.context: Power tastes best when sweetened by courtesy.
sentences.simple: Power works best when it is mixed with politeness.
sentences.grammar: A maxim in taste metaphor: Roose is teaching Ramsay that commands go down easier when wrapped in courtesy — like bitter food made sweet.

sentences.context: Has my bastard ever told you how I got him?
sentences.simple: Has Ramsay ever told you the story of how he was conceived?
sentences.grammar: A chillingly casual question. “How I got him” means how Ramsay came to be born — and the story that follows is a rape.

sentences.context: “Fragrant Steward, rather.”
sentences.simple: It means “Fragrant Steward,” not “Stinky Steward.”
sentences.grammar: Moqorro corrects Tyrion’s rude translation with mock politeness. “Selaesori” means fragrant or sweet-smelling; Tyrion prefers the insulting version.

sentences.context: “Are you speaking of King’s Landing or Volantis?”
sentences.simple: Do you mean the jousting at King’s Landing, or what happened in Volantis?
sentences.grammar: Tyrion asks which disaster Penny blames him for: both. Her brother died because of the chain of events Tyrion set off — first the cruel joust at Joffrey’s wedding, then the drunken sailors in Volantis who killed a dwarf, thinking he was Tyrion.

sentences.context: he knifed me for a squirrel-skin cloak
sentences.simple: He stabbed me to steal a squirrel-skin cloak.
sentences.grammar: 'knife' is used as a verb here: to stab someone with a knife.

sentences.context: Ghiscari slave cities that were old when the world was young
sentences.simple: Slave cities so old they seem as old as the world itself.
sentences.grammar: 'when the world was young' is a poetic way to say 'very long ago' — the world is imagined as a person with a youth.

sentences.context: The more they eat, the larger they will grow
sentences.simple: If they eat more, they will grow bigger.
sentences.grammar: The 'the more... the more...' pattern shows cause and effect: more of the first means more of the second.

sentences.context: she is like to slit his throat on their wedding night
sentences.simple: She will probably cut his throat on their wedding night.
sentences.grammar: Old-fashioned 'like to' + verb means 'likely to' — it does NOT mean 'enjoy' here.

sentences.context: You cannot know what the light might summon from the darkness
sentences.simple: You cannot know what creatures the light might attract out of the dark.
sentences.grammar: Here fire-light is said to 'summon' (call) monsters — the light is given a dangerous, living power.

sentences.context: her blows became moths fluttering about his face
sentences.simple: Her weak hits felt like moths touching his face.
sentences.grammar: A metaphor: her dying punches are compared to moths — light, weak, fluttering things.

sentences.context: Volantis covered the mouth of the Rhoyne like a warm wet kiss
sentences.simple: Volantis lay across the river mouth like a warm, wet kiss.
sentences.grammar: The simile 'like a warm wet kiss' makes the huge city feel unpleasantly soft, close and damp.

sentences.context: A wall is only as strong as the men who stand behind it
sentences.simple: A wall is only strong if brave men defend it.
sentences.grammar: A proverb-like line: 'as strong as' sets up a comparison that carries the real meaning — stone means nothing without men.

sentences.context: Death had lost its terror for Tyrion Lannister, but greyscale was another matter
sentences.simple: Tyrion was no longer afraid of dying, but greyscale still frightened him.
sentences.grammar: 'X was another matter' means X was different — the contrast shows what truly scares him.

sentences.context: He twisted through the bars of his cell and tore his own father apart
sentences.simple: The rumor says the dwarf squeezed through the bars and ripped his father to pieces.
sentences.grammar: This is tavern gossip, not what really happened (Tyrion used a crossbow) — it shows how stories grow wilder as they travel.

sentences.context: Lightbringer was the sun made steel
sentences.simple: The sword Lightbringer shone like the sun turned into metal.
sentences.grammar: A bold metaphor with the verb dropped: 'the sun made steel' = the sun turned into steel.

sentences.context: The word made Dany’s eyes fill up with tears
sentences.simple: Hearing the word 'safe' made Dany start crying.
sentences.grammar: The one-word sentence 'Safe.' just before it lands like a hammer blow — then this sentence explains why the word hurts her.

sentences.context: Only the big one was Little and the little one was Big
sentences.simple: The one called 'Big Walder' was actually the small one, and 'Little Walder' was the big one.
sentences.grammar: A playful reversal: the sentence flips the two names against the two boys — a joke about their confusing nicknames.

sentences.context: Black, he thought, he’s wearing black, he was one of the Watch
sentences.simple: Bran thought: his clothes are black, so he must have been in the Night's Watch.
sentences.grammar: Three short fragments in a row show quick, excited thinking — thoughts don't need full sentences.

sentences.context: The waters of the Rhoyne slowly went from black to blue
sentences.simple: The river water slowly changed color from black to blue as morning came.
sentences.grammar: 'went from black to blue' paints the sunrise as a slow color change, echoing Griff's blue hair in the same paragraph.

sentences.context: I have come through rain and wrack and storm
sentences.simple: I traveled through rain, ruin, and storms to get here.
sentences.grammar: Three heavy nouns in a row ('rain and wrack and storm') sound like an oath — Davos swears he will not turn back now.

sentences.context: Perhaps your elephants would sooner be nightingales
sentences.simple: Your elephants might as well try to become nightingales.
sentences.grammar: An ironic impossible wish: elephants will never be nightingales, so Dany's hope is equally impossible.

sentences.context: That will be wet as well. Dark wings, dark words.
sentences.simple: The raven is wet from the snow, and so will be the letter it carries. “Dark wings, dark words” is a saying: ravens bring bad news.
sentences.grammar: “Dark wings, dark words” is a short rhyming proverb tucked after the observation, stating the general rule that raven-messages mean trouble.

sentences.context: The queen of the rabbits could not be seen without her floppy ears.
sentences.simple: Dany jokes about herself: as the “queen of the rabbits” (a mocking name for her), she must wear her tokar, whose long hanging folds look like rabbit ears.
sentences.grammar: A self-mocking metaphor: the tokar’s draped folds become a rabbit’s “floppy ears,” and Dany casts herself as the “queen of the rabbits.”

sentences.context: that bridge had been burned a long time ago
sentences.simple: Jon destroyed any chance of a life with Val long ago, and he did it himself, by choosing his vows over her.
sentences.grammar: “Burned bridges” is an idiom for a destroyed relationship; the sentence adds the twist that Jon burned it himself, deliberately.

sentences.context: You see Tyrion in every shadow.
sentences.simple: Kevan tells Cersei she imagines her brother Tyrion behind every misfortune, even where he has no part in it.
sentences.grammar: A compact accusation built on a visual metaphor: “in every shadow” means “behind everything bad that happens.”

sentences.context: A man should smell of sweat, not flowers.
sentences.simple: Barristan thinks the perfumed seneschal Reznak is unmanly and untrustworthy: a real man should smell of honest sweat, not perfume.
sentences.grammar: A moral judgment disguised as a rule about smell: “sweat” stands for honest labor, “flowers” for deceitful softness.

sentences.context: too far to let them see that their iron captain had begun to rust
sentences.simple: Far from home, Victarion hides his festering hand wound: his men must not see that their “iron” captain is rotting like rusting metal.
sentences.grammar: An extended metaphor: Victarion is “iron,” so his rotting wound becomes “rust,” decay in the very thing that defines him.

sentences.context: An honor indistinguishable from a death warrant.
sentences.simple: Being made one of Yezzan’s treasured pets is called an honor, but it is really a death sentence: when Yezzan dies, his favorites will have their throats cut.
sentences.grammar: Ironic definition by contradiction: “honor” is redefined as its opposite, a “death warrant,” in a single compressed phrase.

sentences.context: dancing on rotten ice here, them and us. One crack, and we all drown
sentences.simple: Jon warns his officers that the peace with the wildlings is fragile: one violent act by either side, like a crack in thin ice, will kill everyone.
sentences.grammar: A metaphor of collective danger: both sides “dance” together on the same thin ice, so one “crack” drowns them all.

sentences.context: No dragon chair can replace a dragon no matter how elaborately it’s carved.
sentences.simple: Hizdahr’s grand thrones are carved into dragon shapes, but Barristan thinks a wooden dragon is no substitute for a real one.
sentences.grammar: A dry general truth used as political judgment: ornate symbols of power (“dragon chair”) cannot replace the real thing.

sentences.context: Men’s lives have meaning, not their deaths.
sentences.simple: Gerris tells Quentyn that what matters is how his dead friends lived, not how they died; their deaths cannot be given meaning afterward.
sentences.grammar: A philosophical reversal in parallel form: “lives” and “deaths” are balanced against each other to reject Quentyn’s reasoning.

sentences.context: I tried to grasp a star, overreached, and fell.
sentences.simple: Connington sums up his life: he reached too high (for Rhaegar, his “star”), strained beyond his grasp, and lost everything.
sentences.grammar: A three-beat self-epitaph in parallel verbs, compressing a whole life into one image of reaching, straining, and falling.

sentences.context: They had been three days from Winterfell for nineteen days.
sentences.simple: Stannis’s army was supposed to be three days’ march from Winterfell, but the blizzard has held them in place for nineteen days.
sentences.grammar: Bitter irony built on contradiction: the same journey is both “three days” (as planned) and “nineteen days” (in reality).

sentences.context: No man had need of candles when the sun awaited him.
sentences.simple: Victarion keeps the captured girls but does not use them: why settle for candles when the sun, Daenerys, awaits him.
sentences.grammar: A metaphor of desire: lesser pleasures are “candles,” the true prize is “the sun,” making restraint sound like ambition.

sentences.context: He has hands like two white spiders.
sentences.simple: Watching the old man’s constantly moving fingers, Arya thinks they look like two white spiders.
sentences.grammar: A simile that turns restless hands into something creepy and inhuman; it shows her growing hatred, not just their shape.

sentences.context: one day I will have your tongue ripped out with hot pincers
sentences.simple: While speaking meekly to the septa, Cersei is inwardly promising savage revenge: she will have the woman’s tongue torn out with red-hot pincers.
sentences.grammar: The joke structure (“that will be hilarious”) is aimed at a future torture; the humor shows how little her meek act can be trusted.

sentences.context: First, though, you will need to survive what’s coming. No one buys dead mummers.
sentences.simple: Tyrion tells Penny he will find her a kind master after the war, but first she must survive it, because nobody pays for a dead slave-entertainer.
sentences.grammar: A grimly practical punchline: the whole promise depends on the flat commercial truth in the last four words.

sentences.context: It sounds like tears, he thought. It sounds like dead kings, weeping.
sentences.simple: Listening to the rain in the dark, Barristan imagines it sounds like tears, like the dead kings he failed, weeping.
sentences.grammar: A simile built in two steps: rain becomes “tears,” then the tears are given owners, his dead kings.

sentences.context: Never ask the baker what went into the pie. Just eat.
sentences.simple: The Tattered Prince quotes a Pentoshi saying: don’t ask awkward questions about how something was obtained, just accept it.
sentences.grammar: A proverb in two commands: the first forbids the question, the second orders acceptance. Quentyn is told not to ask how the password was learned.

sentences.context: Like a child pulling petals off a daisy, thought Jon.
sentences.simple: Jon watches in horror as the giant Wun Wun tears Ser Patrek’s arm off as easily as a child plucking petals from a flower.
sentences.grammar: A deliberately innocent simile for a gruesome act; the childlike image makes the giant’s casual strength more terrifying.

sentences.context: Not all men are meant to dance with dragons.
sentences.simple: Looking at Quentyn’s burned body, Barristan reflects that some men are not made for such dangerous ambitions; Quentyn should have stayed home.
sentences.grammar: “Dance with dragons” is a metaphor for courting deadly power; the flat “not all men” turns it into an epitaph.

sentences.context: Once I dreamed of flying, she thought, and now I’ve flown
sentences.simple: Starving in the grass, Dany laughs at how desires shrink: she once dreamed of flying, then she flew, and now her dream is stealing birds’ eggs to eat.
sentences.grammar: A three-step ladder of shrinking wishes, flying, flown, eggs, tracing how hunger reduces even a dragonrider’s dreams.

sentences.context: So you say, ser. Words are wind.
sentences.simple: Kevan dismisses Ronnet Connington’s pledge of loyalty: words are empty air; only deeds prove anything.
sentences.grammar: A three-word proverb that deflates the whole preceding speech: talk, however fine, weighs nothing.

sentences.context: I wore many names when I was quick,
sentences.simple: 'Quick' here is an old word for 'alive.' Brynden means: I had many names when I was alive.
sentences.grammar: 'Quick' once meant 'living' — 'the quick and the dead' means the living and the dead.

sentences.context: The oak is the acorn, the acorn is the oak.
sentences.simple: The seed and the old tree are one thing. A tree does not move through time the way men do.
sentences.grammar: The words are flipped for force: the oak IS the acorn. It means start and end are the same to a tree.

sentences.context: the sea of shadow that is all we know of the days to come.
sentences.simple: Men can only live in the now. The past is foggy memory, and the future is dark and unknown.
sentences.grammar: 'The mists of memory' is the past we barely remember. 'The sea of shadow' is the future, which no one can see.

sentences.context: but no man can own both.
sentences.simple: Ygritte's saying: you cannot control a woman and a weapon at the same time. Wildling women are free people.
sentences.grammar: 'Own both' means keep both under your power. The saying warns that free women cannot be owned.

sentences.context: Trouble is the lord commander’s lot, Jon might have said.
sentences.simple: 'Lot' here means one's share in life. Trouble is what a lord commander must live with.
sentences.grammar: 'X is someone's lot' means X is the fate or burden that person is given.

sentences.context: Once for gold and once for blood and once for love.
sentences.simple: The prophecy says Dany will face three betrayals: one for money, one for blood, and one for love.
sentences.grammar: 'Will you know' is old word order for 'you will know.' 'Once for gold' means 'one time, for gold.'

sentences.context: Reek, Reek, it rhymes with meek.
sentences.simple: Theon chants his slave name. 'Meek' means weak and obedient — that is what Ramsay has made him.
sentences.grammar: The rhyme drills the name into his head: Reek rhymes with meek, so he will remember to be obedient.

sentences.context: He would dance this dance for them because he had no choice,
sentences.simple: 'Dance this dance' means play along with their plan. Theon must act his part in Bolton's trick.
sentences.grammar: 'Dance' here means take part in a scheme. 'This dance' is the false-Arya wedding plot.

sentences.context: Be careful, though. King’s Landing is a pit of snakes.
sentences.simple: King's Landing is full of dangerous schemers — like a pit full of snakes waiting to bite.
sentences.grammar: 'A pit of snakes' is a picture: a place crowded with hidden, treacherous people.

sentences.context: Obara, you will lead him to High Hermitage to beard Darkstar in his den.
sentences.simple: 'To beard someone in his den' means to face a dangerous man boldly, in his own home.
sentences.grammar: 'Beard' here means confront face to face. 'His den' is where the man feels strongest.

sentences.context: He let the insult wash right over him.
sentences.simple: Tyrion ignored the insult completely, as if it were water running off his back.
sentences.grammar: 'Let something wash over you' means refuse to let it hurt or move you.

sentences.context: Fire is a fickle thing. No one knows which way a flame will go.
sentences.simple: Melisandre let the baby swap happen because it served her plans. Like fire, she cannot be trusted or predicted.
sentences.grammar: 'It suited her' means it was useful to her. 'Fickle' means changing and untrustworthy.

sentences.context: could eat Ser Justin to break his fast and never even belch.
sentences.simple: Asha means Euron is so much stronger than Justin that he could crush him effortlessly, like eating breakfast.
sentences.grammar: A wild boast: 'eat someone for breakfast' means defeat them with ease. 'Belch' means burp.

sentences.context: Simpler than I dared hope. Simpler than it should have been.
sentences.simple: Jon feels uneasy: the banker's quick agreement seems too easy, too good to be true.
sentences.grammar: The repeated 'simpler' shows Jon's suspicion — an easy deal may hide a trap.

sentences.context: but no one had no tears.
sentences.simple: Arya is becoming 'no one,' and she has no eyes left to cry with. Both meanings are true at once.
sentences.grammar: A wordplay: 'no one' is her new name, and 'no tears' is literal — her eyes were taken from her.

sentences.context: the girl was just a mummer’s ploy, a lamb in a direwolf’s skin.
sentences.simple: The 'Arya' is a fake: a helpless lamb dressed up to look like a Stark direwolf.
sentences.grammar: It twists the saying 'a wolf in sheep's clothing': here the lamb only wears the direwolf's skin.

sentences.context: They certainly were not bidding by the pound.
sentences.simple: Tyrion jokes that the buyers pay so much it is as if the dwarfs were meat sold by weight.
sentences.grammar: Dry humor: 'by the pound' means priced by weight. He pretends the high price is about their bodies.

sentences.context: She is a guest. You are a prisoner.
sentences.simple: Bread and salt is guest right: Alys is a protected guest, but her armed uncle is a prisoner.
sentences.grammar: 'Bread and salt' is the guest ritual. Alys ate it, so she is safe; Cregan never did.

sentences.context: there are bold sellswords, but there are no old bold sellswords.
sentences.simple: Bold sellswords die young, so none grow old. Ben's men left Dany because they did not want to die.
sentences.grammar: A soldier's saying: 'bold' and 'old' never go together, because the bold ones die first.

sentences.context: out of her bed, out of her heart, and out of her.
sentences.simple: Dany cuts Daario off fully: no more lover, no more love, no more place in her rule.
sentences.grammar: Three rising steps — bed, heart, her — each one cuts him out more deeply.

sentences.context: one of the sentries outside the Great Hall japed
sentences.simple: 'Lord Winter' is a joke: winter itself is their ally, and the snowmen are its soldiers.
sentences.grammar: A jape: winter is made into a lord bringing his army — the snowmen on the walls.
